Unit conversions used
\[ P_\text{dBm} = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P_\text{mW}}{1\ \text{mW}}\right) \qquad P_\text{mW} = 10^{P_\text{dBm}/10} \qquad V_\text{rms} = \sqrt{P \times 50\ \Omega} \]

Example: 50 mW = 0.050 W. V rms = √(0.050 × 50) = 1.58 V. In dBm: 10 log10(50) = 17.0 dBm.

Worst case for the splitter: 6.0 dB split loss + 0.5 dB maximum insertion loss (100–2100 MHz) = 6.5 dB.

Limiter

Marki Microwave EVAL-HLM-20P: the HLM-20PSM limiter chip on an SMA evaluation board. Between the RX antenna and the LNA. Keeps strong radar pulses from damaging the LNA.

Specs
QuantityMinTypicalMaxUnit
Frequency rangeDC—20GHz
Insertion loss, DC–20 GHz—0.51.5dB
Insertion loss at 10 GHz (features list)—0.7—dB
Return loss—15—dB
Input power at 1 dB compression—+15—dBm
Flat leakage (output while clamping), at 1 GHz—+17—dBm
Flat leakage, at 20 GHz—+13—dBm
Flat leakage at 9.4 GHz (straight line between the two)—≈ +15—dBm
Spike leakage (energy let through at a pulse’s leading edge)—0.1—erg
Recovery time after a pulse—8—ns
RF power, average, absolute max——5 (+37.0 dBm)W
RF power, peak (pulsed), absolute max——50 (+47.0 dBm)W

Source: HLM-20PSM datasheet, Rev A (electrical specifications, page 4; absolute maximum ratings, page 3) and the EVAL-HLM-20P page. No local PDF: Marki’s site refuses scripted downloads, so open the link in a browser.

The board is marked with an input and an output side. The input side goes toward the antenna. Passive: no power supply.
Expected behavior
  • Below about +10 dBm in, it is a short piece of line: about 0.5–0.7 dB loss at 9.4 GHz.
  • Around +15 dBm in, its diodes start to conduct and the output stops following the input (1 dB compression at +15 dBm in).
  • Well above that, the output stays near the flat leakage, about +15 dBm at 9.4 GHz (+13 to +17 dBm across its band), whatever the input, up to 5 W average and 50 W peak.
  • For each pulse the leading edge gets through before the diodes turn on (spike leakage, 0.1 erg). After the pulse it recovers in about 8 ns.
  • What this means for the LNA (ZX60-5123LN+, absolute max input +15 dBm): the limiter alone does not keep the LNA safe. Put at least 10 dB of pad between them for testing.
\[ P_\text{out} \approx P_\text{in} - 0.5\ \text{dB} \quad (P_\text{in} \ll +15\ \text{dBm}) \qquad P_\text{out} \approx +15\ \text{dBm} \quad (P_\text{in} \gg +15\ \text{dBm at 9.4 GHz}) \]
Test plan

Every step starts with a leak check: the same wiring with a 50 Ω load in place of the antenna. A reading only counts if it is at least 20 dB above that.

Keep 29 dB of pads after the limiter whenever the SM200B is on it: the limiter can pass up to +17 dBm, and the SM200B’s limit is +20 dBm.

  • Loss at 9.4 GHz is about 1.7 dB, against the datasheet’s 0.5 dB typical, 0.7 dB at 10 GHz and 1.5 dB max. The datasheet figures are for the limiter; how much of the extra is the evaluation board was not measured. This replaces the over-the-air 0.8 dB, which was already marked untrustworthy.

Earlier VNA sweep: relative readings, superseded

Screens were in delta-marker mode with an interpolated cal (C2Δ, 1601 points), so these are dB relative to a fixed marker whose value is not on screen. Do not read them as loss. Differences within a column are valid: S21 falls 1.7 dB from 50 MHz to 9.4 GHz. S21 and S12 differ by 0.6–1.1 dB at every marker, more than a reciprocal part should; the 10 dB pad, taken on the same setup, shows the same offset, so suspect the setup. This low-level sweep says nothing about clamping.

The design drawing says “12 V DC operating voltage”. The datasheet operating range is 5 to 10 V, typical 6 V. 12 V is the absolute maximum. Run it at 6 V.

Datasheet. Connectors: SMA female in and out. Internal regulator, reverse-voltage protected.

Expected behavior
  • Draws about 80 mA at 6 V.
  • Adds 22 dB at 9.3–9.5 GHz, flat within ±0.6 dB.
  • Weak radar: −50 dBm in gives −28 dBm out.
  • Strong radar: −10 dBm in gives +12 dBm out. This is below the +17 dBm compression point.
  • Gain starts to drop when the output reaches +17 dBm, which is an input of about −4 dBm.
  • With the input terminated in 50 Ω, output noise is about −150.6 dBm/Hz.
\[ P_\text{out} = P_\text{in} + G \qquad N_\text{out} = -174\ \text{dBm/Hz} + NF + G = -174 + 1.4 + 22 = -150.6\ \text{dBm/Hz} \]
Test plan

Needs a 9.3–9.5 GHz source, the SM200B, fixed attenuators good to 10 GHz, and a supply set to 6.0 V with a 120 mA current limit.

Rules learned: at least 10 dB of pad between the limiter and the LNA (limiter output up to +17 dBm, LNA absolute max input +15 dBm). At 11.5 m from this radar, 20 dB before the LNA keeps it linear. Always measure the leak floor (a 50 Ω load in place of the antenna) for the same wiring first.

Datasheet. Ports: LO = 2, RF = 3, IF = 1. The datasheet conversion loss is measured at a 30 MHz IF. Ours is 1.0–1.2 GHz, so expect some difference.

Expected behavior
  • IF frequency = RF − 8.3 GHz. 9.3 GHz gives 1.0 GHz. 9.5 GHz gives 1.2 GHz.
  • Output is about 7 to 8 dB below the RF input.
  • Weak radar: −28 dBm in gives about −36 dBm out.
  • Strong radar: +12 dBm in. This is above the +5 dBm compression point, so the output will be less than +4 dBm and distorted. It is below the +17 dBm damage limit.
  • LO leaks to the IF port 17 dB down: +10 − 17 = −7 dBm at 8.3 GHz. For a weak radar this is 29 dB stronger than the wanted signal.
  • LO leaks to the RF port 35 dB down: −25 dBm at 8.3 GHz going back toward the LNA.
  • A signal at 7.1–7.3 GHz gives the same IF as 9.3–9.5 GHz. The drawing has no filter before this mixer.
\[ f_\text{IF} = f_\text{RF} - f_\text{LO} \qquad P_\text{IF} = P_\text{RF} - L_c \qquad f_\text{image} = 2 f_\text{LO} - f_\text{RF} \]

Expected behavior
  • Draws about 62 mA at 12 V.

One ZX60-14012L-S+ cannot give +10 dBm to both mixers. It is about 2 dB short even when driven into compression. The drawing shows +10 dBm at each mixer. RX mixer test 3 (conversion loss vs LO power) will show how much the shortfall costs.

  1. Later on 12 Oct the Pluto was connected straight to the spectrum analyzer and its output read at every attenuation setting from 0 to 40 dB, at the same three frequencies and the same tone scale. See the Pluto tab.
  2. The input power at each step is now that measured Pluto level, not the setting.
  3. Gain is the amp output minus the measured Pluto level at the same setting. The low-power gain is the average of the steps below −18 dBm input.
  4. The compression point is the output power where the gain is 1 dB below the low-power gain, found by a straight line between the two nearest steps.
\[ G(A) = P_\text{with amp}(A) - P_\text{Pluto alone}(A) \qquad P_{1\,\text{dB}} = P_\text{out}\ \text{where}\ G = G_\text{low} - 1 \]

Loss measurement

Result

PathPower at analyzer (dBm)Loss of the added part (dB)
VCO → cable A → analyzer7.30—
+ splitter, right output0.606.70
+ splitter, left output0.586.72
+ cable B0.540.04

+ cable D0.510.09

How it was made

  1. 6 Oct. VCO at 5.38 V, 1.0388 GHz.
  2. The VCO was connected to the analyzer through cable A and the power was read.
  3. The splitter was added. The unused output had a 50 Ω load. The power was read again.
  4. Loss = power before minus power after.
  5. Each extra cable was added one at a time and measured the same way.
Delay calculation
\[ \tau = \frac{\Delta L}{v} = \frac{0.114\ \text{m}}{0.7 \times 3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s}} = 0.55\ \text{ns} \]
\[ \Delta\phi = 360^\circ \times f\tau = 360^\circ \times 1.1\times10^{9} \times 0.55\times10^{-9} = 216^\circ \]
  • 4.5 in = 0.114 m. Signal speed in the cable is taken as 0.7 times the speed of light.
  • From 1.0 to 1.2 GHz the phase goes from 196° to 236°.
  • The design drawing asks for 0.2 ns (3 to 4 cm), which gives 90° at 1.1 GHz.
Notes
  • A resistive splitter loses 6 dB per output, not 3 dB. The 6.7 dB measurement is correct. The earlier 1.5 dB reading on 5 Oct was a measurement error.
  • 0.75 W is the maximum rating, not the power flowing. The note of 15 Sep (“750 → 188 → 50 mW”) used the rating as the signal power.
  • Isolation between the outputs is about 6 dB. A reflection from one mixer port reaches the other mixer port 6 dB lower.
  • Not tested: the mixer curve has more turning points than a 0.55 ns delay gives. One possible cause is reflections between the mixer ports through the splitter. A splitter with higher isolation, or attenuators on the mixer ports, would test this.

Phase detector

Mini-Circuits ZX05-30W-S+ mixer, fed by the delay-line splitter. Turns frequency into a DC voltage.

Status, methods and open issues (read this first when coming back to the phase detector; updated 18 Nov)

Goal

One detector voltage per frequency over about 200 MHz, read to ±1–2 MHz after op-amp scaling into an FPGA ADC, whatever the received power. The amplifiers are meant to rail, so every input level should land on the same curve. Absolute frequency does not matter (the PLL shifts it).

Chain as built

Pluto TX → 4 × ZX60-P162LN+ (4.03 V; about 22.5 dB gain and P1dB +19.9 dBm each at 1 GHz, so the chain rails near +20 dBm at every level used) → ZFRSC-42-S+ resistive splitter (about 6 dB between outputs) → every cable from the Pluto through the amplifiers to the splitter is 7 cm (Sorin, 18 Nov) → two arms (LO: cable D 16.6 cm; RF: cable B 15.2 cm + E with adapter ~9 cm; 18 Nov: very short cables, then B and D alone, then 10 dB pads at both mixer ports) → ZX05-30W-S+ LO and RF → IF → SDS1104X-E. Pads at the mixer ports: removed since 15 Nov.

How data is taken and plotted

  • run_pd_overnight.py (run from signal_hound/, system Python): stages written to pd_dither_14nov.csv, one row per reading; tone-off checks as stage off.
  • High-density plan (HD_NIGHT=1 HD_TAG=tag): 600–1600 MHz at −36/−50/−57 dBm, 900–1200 and 1300–1500 MHz first, coarse to fine, then repeats.
  • Each bench configuration is one row in pd_runs.py. make_plots.py redraws every plot from the CSV, rebuilds this site and pushes (--push; --watch during a run).

Expected delay from the arm lengths against the fitted delay (lengths corrected 18 Nov)

Sorin measured B 15.2 cm and D 16.6 cm on 18 Nov; every earlier figure took both as 15 cm. Expected delay = |RF arm − LO arm| / (0.70 c) = 0.0477 ns/cm (velocity factor 0.70 assumed: Amazon SMA cables with a pink jacket, type unknown). Fitted delay: pdlib.delay(f, v, deg=2), 600–1600 MHz, −50 dBm (spread over the three levels ±0.02 ns).

Cable E + adapter, 15 Nov (hdr, ifs)15.2 + 9 − 16.6 = 7.60.380.362.78–2.802.43

  • The 1.4 cm between B and D is 0.07 ns: over 600–1600 MHz it turns the phase by only 24°, so it cannot make the ~360 MHz pattern. The error from the expectation is 2.2–2.5 ns in every run.
  • The fitted delay still tracks the arm difference: C → E → eq changes it by +0.22 and +0.50 ns where the lengths predict +0.14 and +0.43 ns. A straight line through the three runs gives 2.37 ns at zero difference plus 0.058 ns/cm (velocity factor 0.57, residuals ≤0.03 ns): a fixed ~2.4 ns path plus the arm difference, or a slower cable than assumed, or C longer than 12 cm.
  • The fixed part is not in the arm cables: with the same B and D, 10 dB pads at the mixer ports move it from 2.28 to 1.65 ns. It depends on the reflections at the mixer ports.
  • Very short arm cables (sc, 18 Nov) gave 2.76–2.79 ns, the same as cable E; their lengths were not recorded, so that run cannot be placed on the line.

What is known

  • The curve is dominated by a single ~2.3–2.8 ns delay (one cycle per ~360–440 MHz), not the 0.07–0.51 ns the arm differences give (table above).
  • Not the long IF cable (15 Nov), not the Pluto's own level ripple (16 Nov), not the IF termination.
  • SM200B probe of each arm between the splitter and the mixer (18 Nov, 29 dB pads, one mixer port driven, the other terminated): the RF arm with the mixer on it shows 1.9–2.0 dB rms ripple whose strongest delay is 2.72 ns, the detector's delay. With the mixer removed (cable D into an ANNE-50L+) the ripple drops to 0.6–0.8 dB and the 2.7 ns term is gone; with a 10 dB pad at the mixer RF port (19 dB pads to the SM200B) it is 0.56–0.76 dB with no clear delay. So the pattern is the mixer ports' reflection (datasheet VSWR up to 3.5) coming back through the resistive splitter (5.94 dB isolation) into the other arm.
  • Unpadded, each arm carried +10 to +19 dBm (measured + 29 dB), which is what a mixer port receives; the ZX05-30W-S+ RF maximum is +17 dBm (50 mW). With 10 dB pads it is about +2 to +7 dBm.
  • The ZX10-2-1252-S+ (the other splitter on hand) covers 1800–12500 MHz only, so it cannot replace the ZFRSC-42-S+ in this band.
  • Amplifier chain alone into 29 dB of pads (18 Nov, SM200B): railed at +20 to +22 dBm, amplitude ripple ±0.5–0.8 dB with its strongest delay at 4.4 ns, correlation 0.08 with the detector curve; rails over the whole band only with −57 dBm or more in. This does not rule the amplifiers out (Sorin, 18 Nov): it measured amplitude only, into a matched pad, while the 2.75 ns pattern is seen with the amplifiers railed, driving the splitter and mixer, with a 50 Ω IF load. The amplifiers driving the real splitter/mixer load are untested.
  • −50 and −57 dBm agree within about 2 mV; −36 dBm departs on the shoulders (deepest compression; supply current rises to 0.39 A).
  • Best so far: cable E, no pads, rising edge 1340–1480 MHz, about 80 MHz with error ≤2 MHz at ±0.5 mV (−50/−57 dBm). Pads give a smoother but 3× shallower curve.

Open

  • Overnight 18–19 Nov: detector curve with 10 dB pads at both mixer ports, 600–1600 MHz every 1 MHz, −36/−45/−54/−63/−72 dBm (stages pad10_*), to see whether the pads remove the ripple from the detector output itself.
  • Cable C's length (about 12 cm) and the very short cables of the sc run were not measured; the cable velocity factor is unknown.
  • Add a known length (e.g. 15 cm, about 0.75 ns) to one arm: if the fitted delay moves by exactly that, the 2.75 ns is a fixed offset inside the parts; if not, something else sets it.
  • Swap the mixer's LO and RF inputs, then swap in another mixer or splitter, and see whether the delay changes sign or size.
  • A high-isolation (Wilkinson) splitter; a low-pass filter after the amplifiers (the 2nd harmonic is only 5–9 dB down below 800 MHz).

Pitfalls

  • Pluto drops off USB about hourly (Windows logs a bus removal). The scripts resume where they stopped; the wrapper relaunches.
  • sm_api.dll needs the working folder signal_hound/. Use system Python (radioconda has no pyvisa).
  • Never stash, reset or check out while a run writes the CSV (18 Nov: a stash caught the live file; no data lost, but the progress log was cut).
Main result: detector voltage vs frequency, cable E with pads (14 Nov)

Raw detector output, nothing subtracted. Each plot is one run. Top: the cleanest data, the 14 Nov evening run (dithered reading, 50 mV/div), five Pluto levels from the Pluto’s top (−36 dBm) down to −64 dBm, then the same data zoomed on the one-to-one region. Bottom: the widest sweep, 300–4000 MHz at −50 dBm, not dithered (0.2 V/div). Each run sits a few mV higher or lower than the others (see the session-to-session section below), so different runs are not overlaid here.

  • One voltage = one frequency over about 1215–1445 MHz (about 230 MHz). Over 1240–1430 MHz the slope is 0.3–1.2 mV/MHz, median 0.84 mV/MHz (−50 dBm).
  • −36 to −57 dBm agree within ±2 MHz on 90% of 1240–1430 MHz. −64 dBm (faded) is too weak to use.
  • Repeat sweeps on 15 Nov agree with each other to 0.2 mV and with this run to about 1 mV (about 1 MHz).
  • Outside 1150–1550 MHz the curve keeps rippling (the ~375 MHz ripple), so the one-to-one region cannot be widened by going lower or higher.
  • Above 2100 MHz the Pluto has no level table, so the script turned it down by 61 dB: the flat line there is not a detector reading.
All results, most important first
Frequency uncertainty with the power unknown, every run, by one method (Sorin, 19 Nov): need 200 MHz continuous with a total width ≤4 MHz (±2 MHz)

Method (Sorin, 19 Nov). A level set is the Pluto levels from the highest down to a threshold. Its lookup is the median curve: at each frequency, the median of every reading of every level in the set. At each true frequency, take the voltage the detector gives with the input at the top level and at the threshold level (each the median over that level's passes), look both up on the median curve, and plot each frequency read minus the true frequency. The total width is the distance between those two frequencies (±2 MHz = 4 MHz total). The lookup must be single valued, so the median curve is split wherever it turns (increasing or decreasing both fine); a reading past a turn has no unique frequency and is marked × at the bottom. Thresholds: every level (‘could be measuring anything’), −60 dBm, the lowest level where the four ZX60-P162LN+ are railed (what matters, Sorin), and −50 dBm; sets with the same levels are drawn once. Railed = the chain within 1 dB of its saturated output at every frequency 950–1600 MHz in the 18 Nov power ramp (amp_ramp_18nov.csv): −58 dBm is within 0.7 dB, −60 dBm up to 1.1 dB down, −63 dBm 2–3 dB, −72 dBm up to 10 dB, so the railed set is ≥−58 dBm. Each run has two plots: the voltage read against frequency, one line per Pluto level and pass (every reading taken), with the median curves; then the frequency offsets. Script plot_pd_x_uncertainty.py; data pd_dither_14nov.csv (stages per run in pd_runs.py) and p162x4_fine_1nov.csv (cable C).

This replaces the earlier figures (15–19 Nov: pd_resolution_compare.png, pd_power_freq_error_*, pd_power_uncertainty_*). Those used a mean or a monotonic-forced curve, a reading error ±dV added on top, the worst one-sided error, and made-up summaries (best window, % of frequencies, rms). Their numbers should not be used.

Each arrangement in full

Frequency uncertainty for this and every other run: see the first item in this tab, ‘Frequency uncertainty with the power unknown, every run’.

Amplifier chain alone into the SM200B: is the ~360 MHz pattern already in the amplifiers? (18 Nov from 13:06): its amplitude ripple does not match, but that does not rule the amplifiers out (Sorin)

Pluto TX → 4 × ZX60-P162LN+ (4.03 V; every cable 7 cm) → 10 + 10 + 3 + 6 = 29 dB of pads → SM200B. No splitter, arms or mixer. Expected: the chain rails near +20 dBm (datasheet P1dB +19.9 dBm per stage at 1 GHz), so about −9 dBm at the SM200B, nearly the same at every input level. If the amplifiers cause the detector pattern, the output level should ripple with a ~2.75 ns delay (peaks near 770, 1160, 1510 MHz).

Plan: 600–1600 MHz every 25 MHz, then every 5 MHz; Pluto −36, −43, −50, −57, −64, −71 dBm at each frequency. At each point 16384 raw IQ samples (50 MS/s, 328 µs, tone 10 MHz above the centre) are saved, and the instantaneous power |I+jQ|² of every sample is used, not only an average; the 2nd and 3rd harmonics are read too (the Pluto has a line near 3× the tone, 10–16 dB down, and a railed amplifier makes harmonics). Script run_amp_chain_iq.py (wrapper amp_wrapper.sh, waits for the SM200B, resumes after USB drops); data amp_chain_18nov.csv; raw IQ in C:\ThatFamily Dropbox\Sorin Jayaweera\allSaves\mudd\senior\clinic\claude\phase_detector_calibration\amp_chain\ (local only, about 150 MB); plot plot_amp_chain.py.

The Pluto alone, from the Pluto tab (12–13 Oct, into the spectrum analyzer): level repeatable to 0.03 dB on returning to a frequency, settled within 5 ms, and across 600–1600 MHz its ripple after a smooth trend is 0.5 dB rms with only 0.11 dB at a 2.75 ns delay (its strongest component is 1.4 ns, 0.22 dB). With the amplifiers railed that is attenuated further, so the Pluto itself is not the source.

Result (sweep 13:06–13:19, 1206 points): the amplifiers' output level does not carry the detector's ~360 MHz pattern. (Sorin, 18 Nov: this does not rule the amplifiers out; it was measured into a matched pad, not into the splitter and mixer. Later the same day the SM200B arm probes traced the pattern to the mixer ports' reflections; see the 18 Nov section.) With −57 dBm or more into the chain the output is railed at +20 to +22 dBm across 650–1600 MHz, with about ±0.5–0.8 dB of ripple whose strongest single delay is 4.4 ns (about 225 MHz period), not the detector's 2.75 ns; the ripple's correlation with the detector curve (18 Nov short-cable run, 800–1600 MHz, trends removed) is 0.08. Anything before the splitter is common to both arms, so the amplifiers' phase cancels in the detector; only their level could matter, and it does not match. The pattern therefore comes from the splitter, the mixer or the ports between them. It stayed at 2.74–2.77 ns with cable E and with very short arm cables, so it looks fixed inside those parts (for example a different delay from the mixer's LO and RF ports to its core) rather than set by the arm lengths.

Not railed at low input: with −64 dBm in, the output falls to about +18 dBm above 1300 MHz; with −71 dBm it falls from +20 dBm below 1000 MHz to +12 dBm at 1600 MHz. So the chain holds a constant output only down to about −60 dBm at the top of the band; the ramp below maps exactly where.

First readings: the chain puts out +17 to +21 dBm (railed). With no tone it still puts out about −3 dBm in the SM200B's 41.5 MHz window: 90 dB of gain amplifies its own thermal noise, so over the amplifiers' ~1 GHz bandwidth the noise alone is near +6 dBm, close to saturation. Below about 800 MHz the 2nd harmonic lands inside the amplifiers' band and comes out only 5–9 dB under the tone. Where 30.75 dB of Pluto attenuation would be needed (−36 dBm near 1525 MHz) the Pluto script's 31 dB safety floor is used instead, 0.25 dB lower; the CSV keeps the setting used.

Output against Pluto level

After the frequency sweep: Pluto −90 to −36 dBm in 1 dB steps at 700–1600 MHz every 50 MHz plus 770, 960, 1160, 1340 and 1510 MHz (detector peaks and troughs), repeated up to 30 times (rep 1 keeps 16384 IQ samples per point, later reps 4096). Shows where the chain starts to rail, how much of the output is noise rather than tone at each level, and how repeatable it is. Data amp_ramp_18nov.csv, raw IQ amp_ramp\ (local only), wrapper amp_ramp_wrapper.sh (AMP_MODE=ramp).

Pass 1 (all 24 frequencies): the chain rails at +19.5 to +22 dBm everywhere; it is within 1 dB of that from about −70 dBm in below 1000 MHz, but needs −60 to −63 dBm above 1200 MHz. At −90 dBm in the output falls from +11 dBm at 700 MHz to −7 dBm at 1500 MHz.

Gap 14:40–15:11 (rep 9, 750 MHz): the amplifier supply was disconnected at the bench (a status reply was read as “the run is finished”); the SM200B saw only its own floor, not even the amplifiers' noise (tone off −38 dBm against −3 dBm normally). Reconnected unchanged (4.04 V, 0.23 A); resumed 15:11:46. Run stopped at 14:53; the 1689 rows after 14:40:13 were removed (backup backups\amp_ramp_18nov_before_trim_1453.csv, raw IQ moved to amp_ramp\no_signal_1440\). amp_resume.sh probes every 2 min with amp_probe.py and resumes the ramp when the output is back; the run now stops itself if the output at −60 dBm or more drops below 0 dBm.

Very short cables at every mixer connection, 50 ohm load on the IF (18 Nov 10:39-12:40): pattern unchanged

Result (first full pass, 11:02): the pattern did not change. Peaks at −50 dBm at 770, 1160 and 1510 MHz (15 Nov: 760–765, 1162–1164, 1495–1499); best single delay 2.74 ns (15 Nov: 2.77 ns); swing about 450 mV. Tone-off was −8 mV at 10:39 and −25 mV from 11:02 onward, steady after that; the tone-on curve did not move (later passes match pass 1 within about 1 mV median), so only the zero reading changed. So the cables at the mixer and the IF termination are not the source, and nor is any reflection path whose delay is the sum of the arms. New suspect: the amplifier chain itself. Its saturated output power can ripple with frequency (reflections between the four stages), the curve would then be the same at every input level and independent of the arm and IF cables, as seen. Test: amplifier chain output into the SM200B through pads, swept 600–1600 MHz; or drive the splitter straight from the Pluto with the amplifiers bypassed.

Test of whether the ~360 MHz pattern (best single delay about 2.75 ns) comes from reflections on the cables at the mixer. Sorin replaced every connection at the mixer with very short cables and put a 50 ohm load on the IF line into the scope (SDS1104X-E). Same plan as the 15 Nov runs: 600–1600 MHz at −36, −50 and −57 dBm, one reading per point, 100 mV/div; 900–1200 and 1300–1500 MHz filled first, then repeat sweeps every 5 MHz. Data: phase_detector_calibration/pd_dither_14nov.csv, stages sc_pri, sc_rest, sc_rep; tone-off is stage off, reps 141 and up. Plots are redrawn by make_plots.py from the run table pd_runs.py; the comparison with the earlier runs is in the section below.

The ‘ripple’ is the interferometer itself: the arms differ by about 2.75 ns, not 0.55 ns (16 Nov)

Fit of every wide sweep with one delay: V(f) = a + b f + A cos(2π f τ + φ), τ scanned 1.5–4 ns. The ~360 MHz pattern is not a ripple on top of a slow 0.55 ns curve; it is the main term (about 150 mV amplitude), and a 0.55 ns term is not found.

RunRange (MHz)Best τ (ns)Full cycle (MHz)Amplitude (mV)

Cable C, 1 Nov, −60 dBm700–16003.0033369
Cable E, no pads, 13 Nov600–17002.68373125
Cable E, no pads, short IF cable, 15 Nov, −50 dBm600–16002.77361153
  • The delay moves with the arm cable: C to E shortens it by 0.23–0.32 ns. C is about 12 cm and E about 9 cm with its adapter, so 3 cm of coax is about 0.14 ns at velocity factor 0.70. The 2.75 ns is therefore the real difference between the two arms, not an outside reflection.
  • That also explains the usable width: half a cycle of 2.75 ns is about 180 MHz, the one-to-one width seen in every run. A 0.55 ns difference would give about 900 MHz.
  • Ruled out: the long IF cable (same curve with a short one).
  • Cable lengths (Sorin, 16 and 18 Nov): B 15.2 cm, D 16.6 cm (first given as 15 cm each), E about 9 cm with its adapter, C about 12 cm. So the direct arm difference with E is 7.6 cm, about 0.36 ns (velocity factor 0.70 assumed; cable type unknown); it cannot give 2.75 ns.
  • Likely cause: the ZFRSC-42-S+ is a resistive splitter with only about 6 dB between its outputs. A reflection off one mixer port goes back up its arm, crosses the splitter 6 dB down and reaches the other mixer port. Mixed against the direct signal, that path differs by the SUM of the two arms (D + B + E = 40.8 cm, about 1.9 ns of cable, plus the splitter, adapters and the paths inside the mixer to its diodes), not their difference. A sum of arms near 2.75 ns needs about 0.9 ns more than the cables alone, so this is likely but not yet proven.
  • Test that separates the two with no new parts: lengthen arm D only. If the ~360 MHz pattern gets slower (longer cycle), it is the direct difference; if it gets faster, it is the reflection path through the splitter (sum of arms). Fix if it is the reflection path: a high-isolation (Wilkinson or hybrid) splitter in place of the resistive one, or attenuators right at the mixer ports (each dB of pad takes 2 dB off the reflected path).
Is the ~360 MHz pattern the Pluto’s own level ripple? No (16 Nov)

Sorin asked whether the pattern comes from the Pluto, as with the comparator. The Pluto’s output against frequency was measured on 12 Oct straight into the Siglent spectrum analyzer, 350–2090 MHz in 10 MHz steps (pluto_characterization/pluto_map_table.csv; Pluto tab, Results). It has a ripple of its own. Here it is set against the phase detector curve (cable E, no pads, short IF cable, 15 Nov). Script: phase_detector_calibration/plot_pd_vs_pluto_level.py.

  • Pluto ripple: 0.45–0.49 dB rms after a smooth trend, up to about 1.5 dB near 1450 MHz. Its bumps are about 150–200 MHz apart below 1150 MHz and 80–150 MHz apart above; not 360 MHz.
  • Detector sensitivity to the Pluto level: going from −57 to −50 dBm (7 dB) moves the detector by a median 2.9 mV (0.4 mV per dB), at most about 28 mV near 810 MHz and 20 mV near 1500 MHz (about 4 mV per dB). So the Pluto ripple can add at most a few mV; the detector pattern swings by about 500 mV.
  • Correlation between the two after removing smooth trends: |r| ≤ 0.3 at every shift up to ±200 MHz.
  • The pattern also changed with the arm cable (C to E), which a source effect would not do. The Pluto’s line near 3× the tone (10–16 dB down) is still a possible contributor to the shape and to the −36 dBm departure; a low-pass filter after the Pluto would test it.
Short IF cable (15 Nov night): the ~360 MHz ripple is NOT caused by the long IF cable; densest data so far

Test of the idea that the ~360 MHz ripple (about 2.8 ns of delay, far more than the arm difference) comes from reflections on the long IF cable to the scope. Sorin replaced it with an SMA-BNC adapter and an SMA cable about 16 cm long (about twice cable E); nothing else changed (cable E, no pads). Same plan as the long-cable run: 600–1600 MHz at −36, −50 and −57 dBm, one reading per point, 100 mV/div. Data: phase_detector_calibration/pd_dither_14nov.csv, stages ifs_pri and ifs_rest; tone-off readings are stage off, reps 91–93. Plots: plot_pd_ifs.py, plot_pd_hd_night.py ifs. The run went from 20:33 to 21:43 and then stopped when the PC shut down for a Windows update overnight: 1618 readings. 900–1200 and 1300–1500 MHz are complete at 1.25 MHz steps; the rest of 600–1600 MHz is at 5 MHz (2.5 MHz in part).

  • Peaks at −50 dBm: 760, 1162 and 1495 MHz with the long cable; 765, 1164 and 1499 MHz with the short one. The ripple period and positions are unchanged, so the IF cable is not the cause.
  • The swing is about 10–20% larger with the short cable, and the tone-off reading moved from −23.7 to about −45 mV.
  • The levels still lie on top of each other except on the 1100–1150 MHz shoulder at −36 dBm and near the peaks at −57 dBm.
  • Remaining suspects for the 2.8 ns delay: standing waves between the splitter and the mixer ports, or reflections in the shared path before the splitter. The amplifier supply current rose to 0.39 A during this run (0.22 A idle earlier).
Pads removed, long IF cable: 600–1600 MHz at three levels (15 Nov, 20:03–20:31)

Sorin did not trust the 25 MHz no-pads sweeps, so this run fills 600–1600 MHz densely: 900–1200 and 1300–1500 MHz first (5, 2.5, 1.25, 0.625 MHz), then the rest (10, 5, 2.5 MHz). Pluto at −36, −50 and −57 dBm, read back to back at each frequency. One scope reading per point (no dither, as Sorin asked; 2.5 s per point), 100 mV/div because the swing without pads is about 430 mV. The trace noise (about 1.9 mV rms) is half the 4 mV ADC step, so the averaged reading is not stuck on ADC steps. Data: phase_detector_calibration/pd_dither_14nov.csv, stages hdr_pri and hdr_rest. Plot: plot_pd_hd_night.py hdr. Sorin stopped this run after pass 2 to swap in a short IF cable (next section), so it reached 5 MHz in the priority regions and 10 MHz elsewhere.

Pads removed (15 Nov evening): twice the swing, and the curve moves about 110 MHz

Sorin removed the 3 dB pad at the LO port and the 6 dB pad at the RF port; nothing else changed. The same coarse sweep was run twice (1150–1550 MHz every 25 MHz, five Pluto levels, dithered, each sweep with its own 1 min tone-off reading) and compared with the two sweeps taken with the pads that morning.

  • The two no-pads sweeps agree within 0.5 mV (median) at every level, worst 2.0 mV.
  • Swing: about 340 mV peak to peak without pads (−88 to +254 mV, tone-off subtracted) against about 160 mV with them. On the rise the slope is about 2.7–2.8 mV/MHz (25 MHz steps, 1350–1450 MHz), about three times the 0.84 mV/MHz median with pads.

  • −36 to −57 dBm still lie on top of each other; −64 dBm is still off.
  • Tone-off reading: −24.7 mV without pads, −9.9 mV with.
  • The highest raw reading is about 229 mV, close to the top of the scope screen (260 mV) and to the 250 mV stop rule.
Five Pluto levels across 1150–1550 MHz, coarse to fine (14 Nov evening): the rise runs 1215–1445 MHz with no flat sides; −36 to −57 dBm agree within ±2 MHz on 90% of it

Same wiring. Five Pluto levels: −36 dBm (the Pluto's top), −43, −50, −57 and −64 dBm. At each frequency all five are read back to back (seconds apart), so slow drift moves them together. First run (15:50–17:59): 1150–1550 MHz every 2 MHz, stopped at 1412 MHz when the PC crashed. Second run (from 19:14), filled in coarse to fine by halving, as Sorin asked: both ends, the middle, the quarters, … down to 6.25 MHz (1.6% of the 400 MHz span), then 3.1 and 1.6 MHz on the rise only. Each halving step starts by re-reading 1350 MHz at the five levels as a drift check. Every point is dithered (four scope offsets 1 mV apart).

PC crashes, 14 Nov 17:20–18:48

  • 17:19–17:21 and 17:59: the PC entered Modern Standby, logged as “Reason: Lid”; the first run stopped at 17:21 and resumed 17:54 with no lost points.
  • 17:59: hard crash in standby; on restart Windows logged a fatal hardware error (WHEA, processor machine-check record). 18:25, 18:33, 18:37, 18:40: further freezes or forced restarts, some while no measurement was running.

Repeat check, 15 Nov: the curve came back

Same wiring, cables re-checked by hand. Windows Update restarted the PC at 02:01. Two coarse sweeps (1150–1550 MHz every 25 MHz, the same five levels), each a fresh launch of the run script with its own 1 min tone-off reading first.

  • The two sweeps agree to 0.13–0.23 mV (median) at −36 to −57 dBm, worst 0.74 mV; −64 dBm is noisier (up to 5 mV near the peak).

Pluto dropouts (19:38 and 21:51, 14 Nov)

  • Both times Windows logged the Pluto as “surprise removed, missing on the bus”, and the program then lost its connection (Windows error 10053). Nothing was unplugged. The Pluto came back only when its USB hub was reset (19:53) or the PC restarted (02:01).

  • Next: turn off USB power saving for the hub and the Pluto (fix_usb_power_admin.ps1, admin), and log the Pluto's USB state with each failure to tell a Windows-side drop from a Pluto firmware hang.

After a 25 min break: the whole curve moved up about 6 mV (14 Nov 15:29)

The run was stopped at 14:53 and the Pluto replugged; the wiring was not changed (Sorin checked it). On restart the four amplifiers drew 0.26 A instead of 0.23 A at the same 4.03 V. A recheck at 1260, 1300, 1340, 1380 and 1420 MHz at all seven levels read 5.4 to 7.6 mV higher than before at every level from −56 to −36 dBm (−60 dBm: −0.6 to +6.0 mV). The tone-off reading moved only 0.3 mV, so the change is in the detector's response, not the scope. As frequency that is 5 to 13 MHz, far outside ±2 MHz; but the shift is nearly the same at every level, so the power dependence did not change: the whole curve moved. A shift like this can be removed by calibrating against one known tone. With the tone off the IF port showed a comb of lines on multiples of 40 MHz from 1200 to 1680 MHz, up to about −35 dBm at the IF port (spectrum in if_toneoff_spectrum_14nov_1530.csv; source not known, 40 MHz is the Pluto's reference clock). Finer power-level passes (4, 2, then 1 MHz) are running to follow it.

Reading the detector in the 700 ns budget: op-amp scaling stage 0.5–2.0 V, op-amp choice, timing (14 Nov)

The racon has 700 ns from receiving a radar pulse to sending the reply, so the detector voltage is read once (or averaged over a few samples) and used at once. Dithering as done on the scope is a bench fix only. In the real front end a gain stage makes the ADC step small against the slope, and the stage's own noise smooths the steps.

Scaling stage

Detector 0 to 160 mV (the 1228–1440 MHz rise) to 0.5 to 2.0 V: Vout = 0.5 V + 9.375 Vin. Two halves of a dual op-amp, 3.3 V single supply: A is a unity-gain buffer on the detector (so the offset resistors do not pull about 30 µA into the mixer IF port); B is non-inverting, with the buffer output through R1 and 3.3 V through R2 summed at the + input, Rg from − to ground, Rf from output to −.

PartSlow op-amp (MCP6002)Fast op-amp (OPA2356 etc.)Job
R11.62 kΩ162 Ωbuffer output to + input
R2100 kΩ10 kΩ3.3 V to + input (sets 0.5 V)
Rg1.2 kΩ120 Ω− input to ground
Rf10.2 kΩ1.02 kΩoutput to − input
  • Gain 1 + Rf/Rg = 9.5; 0 mV gives 0.500 V, 160 mV gives 1.996 V; 8.0 mV per MHz at the ADC.
  • On 5 V: R1 = 1.07 kΩ (107 Ω), the rest unchanged.
  • The offset comes from the supply: 10 mV of supply noise moves the output about 1.6 mV (0.2 MHz). A reference (e.g. LM4040) is better.
  • Out of band the detector reaches about 180 mV, i.e. 2.2 V out: clamp or check the ADC input limit.
  • 1% resistors give up to about 2% gain error (about ±2 MHz across the band); the look-up table must be measured through this exact stage, which calibrates it out.

  • Noise: the scope saw about 0.8 mV rms per sample with the tone on (20 MHz bandwidth), about 0.9 MHz rms per sample. Averaging 4 samples gives about 0.47 MHz rms, 8 samples about 0.33 MHz rms.
  • After the ×9.5 stage that noise is about 8 mV rms at the ADC, about one step of an 8-bit 2 V ADC (7.8 mV), enough to smooth the steps when averaging.

Delay cable E (about 9 cm with its adapter) with pads at the mixer ports, 13–14 Nov: voltage vs frequency, power levels, noise, drift

Goal: one clean voltage per frequency over 200 MHz, read to ±2 MHz. The PLL can move the band anywhere, so the absolute frequency does not matter. Wiring (every plot shows it): Pluto TX → 4 × ZX60-P162LN+ (4.03 V, 0.23 A) → ZFRSC-42-S+ → right arm cable D to the LO port, left arm cable B + E to the RF port → ZX05-30W-S+ → IF to SDS1104X-E CH1 (1 MΩ) and, through pads, the SM200B. D is 16.6 cm and B 15.2 cm (Sorin, 18 Nov; earlier taken as equal), so the RF arm is longer by E + B − D = 9 − 1.4 = 7.6 cm. On 1 Nov it was cable C (about 12 cm), 10.6 cm.

Cable C against cable E, and pads at the mixer (13 Nov)

With C and with E the output ripples about every 375 MHz, which a few-cm length difference cannot cause (it would give a period of a few GHz). The guess was reflections between the badly matched mixer ports and the splitter; the 31 Oct VNA data shows the RF port at −6 dB return loss at 1.5 GHz and the LO port at −13.7 dB. A 3 dB pad was put at the LO port and a 6 dB pad at the RF port (a pad improves the match by twice its value, so both ports end near −18 to −20 dB). The swing shrank about 3× and one clean rise appeared from 1228 to 1440 MHz (212 MHz).

Power levels in the band (1 Nov, 13 Nov evening and 14 Nov)

1 Nov (cable C, no pads): 1 MHz sweeps at −70, −65, −60, −50, −40 and −36 dBm; from 960 to 1010 MHz the levels from −65 to −36 dBm differ by 10.8 mV on average, about 4 MHz. 13 Nov evening: 2 MHz steps at −50 dBm with −60 and −55 dBm passes (the −45 and −40 dBm passes were lost when the Pluto dropped off USB). 14 Nov: a power ramp from −80 to −36 dBm in 2 dB steps at ten frequencies from 1225 to 1450 MHz. From about −58 dBm up the output does not change with level at any frequency: the detector is saturated, so at −50 dBm the reading depends on frequency only. Below −60 dBm it falls with level.

Whole range, 300–4000 MHz, with the IF port on the SM200B (14 Nov)

10 MHz steps from 300 to 4000 MHz and 5 MHz steps from 600 to 2100 MHz. The 5 MHz sweep lies on the 13 Nov sweep within a few mV. Above 2090 MHz the output is zero because the Pluto level table stops there and the attenuation is set for the worst-case output, so the real level is far below −50 dBm (the IF tone drops by about 20 dB at the same point). The IF port carries the tone at about −12 dBm and 2f at about −10 dBm in the band (referred to before the 20 dB of pads).

Findings

  • The staircase in the slope (about 9.3 MHz period) is the scope, not the detector: every flat step sits on an exact multiple of 8.0 mV, one ADC step at 0.2 V/div, and the noise (0.3 mV) is too small to smooth across steps. At 50 mV/div (2 mV steps) the steps were still there, 2.0 mV apart. From 13:01 every point is read at four scope offsets 1 mV apart and averaged (dither); the staircase is gone (see the next section). A reading front end needs an ADC step well under 8 mV.
  • Hold at 1340 MHz for 20 min: sd 0.33 mV, no visible drift. Tone off: sd 0.26 mV.
  • Between 13 Nov evening and 14 Nov midday the band sits 2 to 7 mV higher. That is session-to-session drift, not noise.
  • Slope in 1240–1430 MHz from the dithered sweep: 0.17 to 1.19 mV/MHz, median 0.82 mV/MHz (the 0.54 mV/MHz read at 0.2 V/div was pulled down by the staircase).

Output voltage vs frequency, VCO source

Result

  • Rises from 30.3 mV at 743.6 MHz to 121.3 mV at 788.4 MHz.
  • Then: minimum 111.4 mV at 802.2 MHz, maximum 145.7 mV at 834.2 MHz, minimum 136.0 mV at 868.0 MHz, maximum 142.1 mV at 886.0 MHz.
  • Above 788 MHz one voltage matches more than one frequency.

How it was made

  1. Same sweep as the VCO frequency measurement. At each of 176 tuning voltages:
  2. the analyzer read the VCO frequency,
  3. scope CH2 read the mixer output. Three records of 14 ms each were averaged.
  4. The mixer voltage is plotted against the frequency from the analyzer.

Expected shape

\[ V_\text{out} \approx V_0 + A\cos(2\pi f\tau) \]

With τ = 0.55 ns this is one slow curve with turning points 900 MHz apart. The measured curve has turning points 14 to 34 MHz apart. The cause was not found.

  • At −12.25 dBm: minimum near 1.03 GHz, maximum at 1.20 GHz.

How it was made

  1. September. Pluto SDR → splitter → two cables → mixer → multimeter.
  2. The Pluto frequency was stepped by hand in 5 MHz steps and the multimeter read at each.
  3. This was repeated at four Pluto power settings.

Right plot, 10 October

  • This is the computer-run sweep. The Syscomp stepped the VCO tuning pin from 0 to 3.5 V in 0.02 V steps, 176 points.
  • At each step the spectrum analyzer read the VCO frequency (x axis). Scope CH2 read the mixer IF output into 1 MΩ, averaged over three 14 ms records (y axis).
  • The Syscomp reaches 3.52 V at most, so the sweep covers 744 to 920 MHz. That is below the 1.0 to 1.2 GHz band the JACON uses.
  • Green band, 744 to 788 MHz: the output only rises, 30 to 121 mV, so each voltage matches one frequency. Above 788 MHz it turns at 802, 834, 868 and 886 MHz, so one voltage matches several frequencies.
  • A 0.55 ns delay alone gives turning points 900 MHz apart, not 14 to 34 MHz apart. The cause is not known.
  • The +0.6 dBm per mixer port in the legend was measured after the splitter on 6 Oct at 1.04 GHz. It was not measured again during this sweep.
  • The two plots are different bands, sources and powers. They are not the same curve.

Mixer look up table

Result

  • Valid from 743.6 to 788.4 MHz, 30.3 to 121.3 mV.
  • Point-to-point roughness 0.084 mV = 40 kHz.
  • Slope 0.05 to 3.73 mV/MHz. Below 755 MHz and above 785 MHz the slope is small, so a small voltage error is a large frequency error.

How it was made

  1. Take the 61 calibration points with tuning voltage 0 to 1.2 V. In this range the mixer voltage only rises with frequency.
  2. Left panel: these points, frequency on the x axis, voltage on the y axis.
  3. Middle panel: the same points with the axes swapped.
  4. To convert a voltage, find the two points on either side of it and draw a straight line between them.
  5. Right panel: the slope between neighbouring points.
\[ f(V) = f_i + (V - V_i)\,\frac{f_{i+1} - f_i}{V_{i+1} - V_i} \qquad \delta f = \frac{\delta V}{dV/df} \]
Code
use = cal[cal["vt_meas_v"] <= 1.2]             # the part where voltage only rises with frequency
mhz, mv = use["vco_freq_hz"] / 1e6, use["mixer_out_v"] * 1e3
order = np.argsort(mv)

def mv_to_mhz(x):
    return np.interp(x, mv[order], mhz[order])

Full table: see the Look up tables tab.

Step response

Result

  • The mixer output follows each step. 10–90 % time 89 to 140 ns rising, 93 to 128 ns falling.
  • The drive voltage takes 145 ns and has a spike at the start. The mixer is responding to that shape.

How it was made

  1. The Syscomp drove the VCO tuning pin with a 50 kHz square wave. Low level 0.2 V. High level 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0 or 1.15 V.
  2. The scope recorded the drive (CH1) and the mixer output (CH2) for 2.8 ms. That holds about 140 rising and 140 falling edges. Three recordings per step.
  3. The time of each edge was found from where the drive crossed half-way between its low and high levels.
  4. All the edges were shifted to the same time zero and stacked on top of each other, then averaged. About 420 edges per curve. Averaging reduces the noise by about 20 times.
  5. Top panel: average drive voltage. Middle panel: average mixer voltage. Bottom panel: the mixer voltage converted to frequency with the look up table.
  6. These are the recorded signals. Nothing has been divided out.
\[ \bar{y}(\tau) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N} y(t_k + \tau) \qquad N \approx 420 \]
Code
dlo, dhi = levels(vd)                          # low and high level of the drive
edges = rising_edges(t, vd, dlo, dhi)          # time of each 50 % crossing

def stack_edges(t, y, edges, grid):            # grid = times relative to an edge
    acc, n = np.zeros(len(grid)), 0
    for e in edges:
        acc += np.interp(grid + e, t, y)       # this edge, shifted to time zero
        n += 1
    return acc / n                             # average of all edges
Time to within 2 MHz of the final frequency

Result

Step on Vt (V)Mixer (mV)Frequency (MHz)Within 2 MHz, after drive 50 % (ns)Within 2 MHz, after drive starts (ns)
0.20 → 0.4035.8 → 54.7752.9 → 763.274122
0.20 → 0.6036.0 → 75.2753.1 → 771.2100148
0.20 → 0.8036.2 → 97.7753.4 → 777.9110158
0.20 → 1.0036.4 → 115.3753.6 → 783.6114162
0.20 → 1.1536.1 → 121.1753.2 → 787.2122170
  • Falling steps: 82 to 164 ns after the drive 50 % point.
  • After entering the band the frequency stays inside it. There is no overshoot.

How it was made

  1. Start from the averaged step traces.
  2. Left column: the measured mixer voltage. Right column: the same trace converted to frequency with the look up table.
  3. The final frequency is the median of the trace from 3 to 4.5 µs after the edge.
  4. The green band is the final frequency ±2 MHz. On the left it is converted back to mV with the look up table.
  5. The red dot is the first sample inside the band.
\[ t_\text{in} = \min\{\, t : |f(t) - f_\text{final}| \le 2\ \text{MHz} \,\} \]
Code
fr = mv_to_mhz(mixer_mv)                       # mixer trace converted to frequency
f_final = np.median(fr[(t > 3000) & (t < 4500)])   # ns after the edge
inside = np.abs(fr - f_final) <= 2.0           # MHz
t_first = t[np.nonzero(inside & (t > -150))[0][0]]
10–90 % time vs step size

How it was made

  1. For each averaged trace, take the start level and the end level.
  2. Find the time it reaches 10 % of the way and the time it reaches 90 % of the way. The difference is the 10–90 % time.
  3. This was done for the drive voltage, the mixer voltage and the converted frequency.
  4. The mixer and frequency times differ because the look up table is curved.
\[ s(t) = \frac{y(t) - y_0}{y_1 - y_0} \qquad t_r = t(s{=}0.9) - t(s{=}0.1) \]
Deconvolution

Result

  • Gain is within 1 dB of flat up to 3 MHz.
  • Delay 26 ns.
  • The step response of the part alone rises in 68 ns. A perfect part measured the same way also gives 68 ns. So the part is faster than this measurement can show.
  • Valid only up to 7 MHz. The drive edge has almost no content near 10 MHz, so the division gives a false peak there (grey area).

How it was made

  1. The recorded mixer output is the response of the part to the Syscomp edge, which is slow and has a spike. The aim is the response to a perfect step.
  2. First remove the curve of the look up table: convert each mixer trace back to the tuning voltage that gives that mixer voltage. Now input and output are both in volts and the gain is 1.
  3. Differentiate the drive and the output. A step becomes a pulse.
  4. Take the Fourier transform of both.
  5. Divide the output transform by the drive transform. This undoes the convolution and gives the transfer function of the part. All 20 steps are combined in the division.
  6. Multiply by a 7 MHz low-pass filter, inverse transform, and integrate. This gives the step response of the part alone.
  7. Bottom right panel: grey is the recorded drive, blue is the recorded output (the raw system response), red is the step response of the part with the drive divided out, dotted is a perfect part through the same 7 MHz filter.
\[ H(f) = \frac{\sum_i X_i'^{*}(f)\, Y_i'(f)}{\sum_i |X_i'(f)|^2} \qquad s(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{t} \mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\left\{ \frac{\sum_i X_i'^{*} Y_i'}{\sum_i |X_i'|^2 + \lambda}\, G(f) \right\} dt' \]

X′ and Y′ are the transforms of the differentiated drive and output. λ is 2 % of the value at zero frequency. G is the 7 MHz low-pass. Delay is the slope of the phase below 5 MHz.

\[ \tau = -\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{d\phi}{df} \]

Scope CH1 was connected part-way along the cable to the VCO, so the recorded drive is not exactly the voltage at the tuning pin. This may be why the gain rises above 0 dB between 3 and 7 MHz.

Code
xn = normalise(drive)                          # drive, scaled 0 to 1
yn = normalise(mixer_to_vt(mixer_mv))          # mixer output converted back to tuning volts, scaled 0 to 1
DX = np.fft.rfft(np.gradient(xn) * win)        # differentiate, then Fourier transform
DY = np.fft.rfft(np.gradient(yn) * win)
Sxx = mean over the 20 steps of |DX|^2
Sxy = mean over the 20 steps of conj(DX) * DY
H = Sxy / Sxx                                  # output divided by input
H_reg = Sxy / (Sxx + 0.02 * Sxx[0])            # same, with a small number added so it cannot divide by zero
step = np.cumsum(np.fft.irfft(H_reg * G))      # G = low-pass at 7 MHz; cumsum integrates the impulse response

The values include the scope noise, so the part itself is quieter.

How it was made

  1. The tuning voltage was held fixed, waveform off.
  2. Scope CH2 was set to AC coupling, 1 mV/div, and recorded 1.4 ms.
  3. The rms of the record is the voltage noise.
  4. CH3 with nothing connected was recorded with the same settings. That is the scope noise.
  5. Voltage noise divided by the look up table slope at that frequency gives frequency noise.
  6. For the 1 MHz and 100 kHz columns the record was low-pass filtered first.
\[ \sigma_f = \frac{\sigma_V}{dV/df} \qquad \text{example: } \frac{137\ \mu\text{V}}{3.64\ \text{mV/MHz}} = 38\ \text{kHz} \]
Drift over 74 minutes

Result

  • Middle panel. At 1.0 to 1.6 V the mixer output fell steadily, by 0.4 mV per hour at most.
  • At a fixed frequency in the 744–788 MHz range the output changed by at most 0.37 mV. 0.37 mV / 2.66 mV/MHz = 140 kHz.

How it was made

Same 18 sweeps and same method as the VCO drift plot. Each cell is one reading minus the median for that voltage.

Notes

Measured

  • The output depends on input power as well as frequency. The look up table is valid only at the power it was measured at.
  • The LO port had +0.6 dBm. The datasheet level is +7 dBm.
  • All scope readings were into 1 MΩ. A 50 Ω load on the IF port will give a different voltage.

From the datasheet

  • RF port VSWR 2.8 to 3.5 near 1 GHz. LO port 1.7 to 2.0.
  • LO–IF isolation 7 dB minimum, so some RF appears on the output.

Consequences

  • The RF limiting amp in the design keeps the power fixed. Without it a strong and a weak radar give different voltages at the same frequency.
  • The limiting amp output must be under +23.5 dBm: mixer limit +17 dBm plus 6.5 dB splitter loss.
  • The mixer has never received more than about 3 mW. Its limit is 50 mW.

Datasheet. Ports: LO = 1, RF = 2, IF = 3. No supply needed. The datasheet does not specify DC output when used as a phase detector.

Expected behavior
  • Both inputs are the same frequency, so the IF output is a DC voltage.
  • The voltage follows a cosine of the phase difference between the two inputs.
  • With a 0.55 ns cable difference the phase is 196° at 1.0 GHz and 236° at 1.2 GHz. The voltage should change smoothly in one direction across the band.
  • The voltage also scales with input power. It is only a frequency reading if the power is held fixed.
\[ V_\text{out} \approx V_0 + A(P)\cos(2\pi f\tau) \qquad \tau = 0.55\ \text{ns} \]
Test plan
  1. Output vs frequency with the Pluto at four power levels, by hand. Done in September.
  2. Output vs frequency with the VCO as source, by computer, 744 to 920 MHz. Done 10 Oct.
  3. Step response, noise and drift. Done 10 Oct.
  4. Not done: the same in 1.0–1.2 GHz, with fixed power, and with different delay cables. See Tests to run, PD1 to PD5.

Phase detector step response (10 Oct): VCO tuning stepped between two voltages, detector output against time

The VCO tuning voltage was stepped between a low and a high value (0.2 to 1.15 V) and the phase detector output was captured on the scope, three shots per step. The plots show the mean trace per step, rise and fall, the time to settle within 2 MHz, and the transition time against voltage.

Script phase_detector_calibration/deconvolve.py says:

Deconvolution: divide the drive's edge shape out of the measured step responses.

Input  x(t): drive voltage on Vt (scope CH1), averaged over ~420 edges.
Output y(t): mixer voltage (scope CH2), converted back to "equivalent Vt" with the static
             calibration so that the static nonlinearity of VCO + mixer is removed and what is
             left is a linear system with a DC gain of 1.
H(f) = cross-spectrum(x', y') / power-spectrum(x'), combined over all 20 recorded steps
(the derivatives are used so the signals are pulse-like and can be Fourier transformed).
The deconvolved step response is the running integral of the inverse transform of H(f),
band-limited to where the drive edge actually has energy.

Script phase_detector_calibration/deconvolve.py says:

Deconvolution: divide the drive's edge shape out of the measured step responses.

Input  x(t): drive voltage on Vt (scope CH1), averaged over ~420 edges.
Output y(t): mixer voltage (scope CH2), converted back to "equivalent Vt" with the static
             calibration so that the static nonlinearity of VCO + mixer is removed and what is
             left is a linear system with a DC gain of 1.
H(f) = cross-spectrum(x', y') / power-spectrum(x'), combined over all 20 recorded steps
(the derivatives are used so the signals are pulse-like and can be Fourier transformed).
The deconvolved step response is the running integral of the inverse transform of H(f),
band-limited to where the drive edge actually has energy.

Envelope detector

Analog Devices ADL5511 on the ADL5511-EVALZ board. Takes one output of the IF splitter (1.0–1.2 GHz) and gives a voltage that follows the size of the IF signal. The comparator after it decides “radar pulse present”.

Specs
QuantityMinTypicalMaxUnit
Frequency rangeDC—6GHz
Supply VPOS4.755.05.25 (5.5 absolute max)V

Input on the eval board—≈ 50 Ω (75 Ω shunt R5 with the chip’s 250 Ω), 100 pF AC coupling—

Datasheet (Rev. E): Table 1 specifications, Table 2 absolute maximum ratings, eval board section. Eval board: VPOS and GND pins; RFIN and VENV on SMA; EREF, VRMS and GND on clip-on test points (their SMA pads are empty); SW1 toward its label = enabled.

VENV sits at about 1.1 V with no signal. Into 50 Ω that is 22 mA, more than its 15 mA drive. Never terminate VENV in 50 Ω: scope inputs at 1 MΩ, short cable.
Expected behavior
  • The output follows the RF voltage, not the power: 5 dB more input = ×1.78 more output.
  • At about 1.1 GHz the gains are 1.47 V/V (VENV) and 1.91 V/V (VRMS), interpolated between the 900 MHz and 1.9 GHz datasheet columns. Across 1.0–1.2 GHz they change by about 0.1 dB, so the detector is flat over the IF band.
  • VENV follows each pulse (4 ns rise). VRMS is averaged and gives the mean power.
\[ V_\text{ENV} - V_\text{EREF} = 1.47\,V_\text{in,rms} \qquad V_\text{RMS} = 1.91\,V_\text{in,rms} + V_\text{offset} \qquad V_\text{in,rms} = \sqrt{10^{P_\text{dBm}/10}\cdot 1\,\text{mW}\cdot 50\,\Omega} \]
Input (dBm)−30−20−100+10+17
VENV − EREF (mV)103310332710302310
VENV (V), EREF = 1.1 V1.111.131.201.432.133.41

Level at the detector in the JACON

  • The drawing gives −36 to +4 dBm at the IF amp input. With the ZX60-P103LN+ (+15.6 dB) and the IF splitter (6.0–6.5 dB loss) the detector sees about −27 to +14 dBm.
  • The weakest radar is then only about 3 dB above the detector’s floor (−30 dBm, measured), and the strongest is 3 dB under its +17 dBm limit.
  • At +14 dBm VENV is about 2.7 V. The comparator (ADCMP604) needs its supply at 3.3 V or more to accept that (input max VCC + 0.5 V).
\[ P_\text{det} = P_\text{IF amp in} + 15.6 - (6.0\ \text{to}\ 6.5) = -36 + 15.6 - 6.5 = -26.9\ \text{dBm} \quad\text{to}\quad +4 + 15.6 - 6.0 = +13.6\ \text{dBm} \]
Test plan

Bench: Pluto TX (1.0–1.2 GHz tone, up to about 0 dBm) straight into RFIN. Supply 5.00 V with a 60 mA limit. VENV to Syscomp CGR-201 input A. VRMS to a multimeter (26 Oct) or CGR-201 input B (1 Nov). EREF on a multimeter. Procedure with fill-in tables: envelope_detector/ED-TEST-PROCEDURE.md.

  1. Pluto (Soapy sink, Homebrew GNU Radio) set to a tone 100 kHz above its LO, tone scale 0.7, at 1100 MHz. The script turned it on at 89 dB attenuation and stepped down to 0 dB.
  2. At each step it waited 1 s, then averaged three CGR-201 captures (12 288 samples, 156 kHz sampling) of VENV on input A. VENV rise is the mean minus the mean before the Pluto was turned on (1.1412 V).
  3. VRMS was read on a multimeter at each step and typed in. Its offset with no signal, 31.4 mV, is the mean of the 89 to 50 dB rows.
  4. Power at RFIN: both outputs, at 10, 5 and 0 dB attenuation, with the datasheet gains, give the Pluto level. Every other row is that minus the attenuation (the AD9364 steps are exact: setting the gain and reading back the register gave −89.0, −79.0, 0.0 dB).
  5. VENV gain is the VENV rise divided by the input voltage at that power.
\[ V_\text{in} = \frac{V_\text{RMS} - 31.4\ \text{mV}}{1.91} \;\text{or}\; \frac{V_\text{ENV,rise}}{1.47} \qquad P_\text{RFIN} = -A - 0.02\ \text{dBm} \quad (\text{worst disagreement } 0.24\ \text{dB}) \]

What it shows

  • The detector meets its datasheet at 1.1 GHz: gain 1.47–1.51 V/V from −10 to 0 dBm; 25.6 mV at −20 dBm against the datasheet’s 26 mV.
  • Below about −15 dBm VENV falls under the straight line 1.47 × Vin: 2 dB low at −20 dBm, 5 dB low at −30 dBm. Use the measured curve, not the formula, to set comparator thresholds.
  • Usable range on this bench: −30 dBm (detector floor) to 0 dBm (the most this Pluto gives at tone scale 0.7).
  • VENV scatter seen by the CGR-201: 2 mV rms with no signal, rising to 13.7 mV at 0 dBm (4 %). Checked on 1 Nov: a 400 kHz line from the Pluto, not the detector (see below). It averages out here, but the comparator sees it sample by sample.
  • EREF and VENV fell 10 mV while the board warmed up, then held within 1–2.4 mV over the 10-minute sweep.
Under question: the detector puts the Pluto at 0.0 dBm (tone scale 0.7, 0 dB, 1100 MHz). The Pluto tab measured −0.36 dBm at tone scale 0.5 on the spectrum analyzer, which predicts +2.6 dBm at 0.7. The 2.6 dB difference is not explained: a different Pluto sample scaling in the Soapy driver (the Pluto tab used libiio), this detector’s gain being low, or the cable. Next check: run the same Soapy flowgraph into the spectrum analyzer.
1 Nov: the runs on 1 Nov used a different Pluto (serial …dfdb; 26 Oct …41f6), which reads 0.4 dB lower through the same detector, so part of the difference may be between Pluto units. Still open: every dBm on this tab rests on the detector’s datasheet gains until the spectrum analyzer check is done.

  2. With no RF, read VENV (CGR-201 or meter).
  3. Set the comparator threshold to that value plus the margin. Start at +20 mV: ten times the drift once warm.

1 Nov: band edges, pulse response, extra checks

  • Different Pluto from 26 Oct: serial …dd1f84bfdb (26 Oct: …f3647c41f6). The same 1.1 GHz sweep read 0.44–0.49 dB lower at every level, and the ratio of the two detector outputs was unchanged, so the difference is the Pluto. The “TX level → dBm” calibration is per Pluto unit; ed_sweep.py now writes the serial into every CSV.
  • Long RF cable Pluto → RFIN for the runs below, after a short cable gave intermittent RF at three steps (that run is kept as …_INTERMITTENT-RF_do-not-use.csv). Re-seating the SMA and repeating 0 and −10 dB gave the same readings within 0.03 dB.
  • VRMS read on CGR-201 input B instead of the meter; EREF read on the meter before and after each run (1.137 → 1.136 V, 0.0 mV drift within each run).
Limitation, CGR-201 input B (VRMS): its absolute readings are only good to several mV. Against the meter it read 1.4–1.7 % low, and its offset drifted from −7.5 to −2.5 mV over 75 minutes. Hook on GND repeated within 1 mV, and swapping the leads showed the error stays with input B, so it is calibration, not wiring. Every VRMS value below is a rise (reading minus that run’s no-RF reading), which cancels the offset; the gain error is about 0.15 dB. Input A (VENV) read 4–8 mV above the meter’s EREF.

  1. At each level the script measured CW, then switched the Pluto to pulses (2 MS/s, on and off for the same time) and the CGR-201 to 2.5 MS/s (100 µs) or 20 MS/s (10 µs).
  2. Pulse height: mean of the flat top minus the mean between pulses, skipping the edges (edges found on a smoothed copy with hysteresis). Checked first on synthetic captures with known heights: within 0.3 mV.

  • Between pulses VENV returns to within 0.1–3.5 mV of the no-RF level, well under a +20 mV threshold.

CheckResult
VENV ripple source (CW, TX 0 dB)One line at 400 kHz, 13.7 mV peak, and 800 kHz (1.2 mV). Not there with RF off (only lines near 70 kHz under 1 mV). 400 kHz is 4 × the 100 kHz tone offset: the tone beating with a Pluto TX spur at −300 kHz, about −25 dBc. From the Pluto, not the detector.
10 µs pulse shape (40 MS/s, 9 pulses averaged)10–90 % edges 0.65 µs (the Pluto at 2 MS/s). Overshoot at both edges and ringing before each rising edge, which only a digital filter can do: the Pluto’s. The top wobbles ±2–3 % with the 400 kHz ripple, which is locked to the pulses. The 10 µs shortfall above is this, not the detector.
Input B: calibration or faultHook on GND −2.0 to −3.2 mV, repeatable within 1 mV; with the leads swapped the error stays with input B. Calibration.
RF connector re-seated0 dB: 258.2 mV (257.5–258.1 before); −10 dB: 79.0 mV (78.7–78.9). Within 0.03 dB
Unverified: that the 400 kHz ripple comes from the Pluto’s −3 × f spur. Its frequency is locked to the tone offset, which points that way; changing the offset to 150 kHz should move it to 600 kHz. Until then, treat the mechanism as likely, not shown. For the comparator test: at full Pluto output VENV carries ±14 mV of ripple and the pulses overshoot about 15 % at their edges. Keep the threshold well under the pulse top.
  • Not done: the detector’s own 4 ns rise and 50 ns–1.2 µs pulses (needs the Pluto at a higher sample rate and the oscilloscope); an absolute power check of the Pluto and cable on the spectrum analyzer.

Comparator

Analog Devices ADCMP604 on the EVAL-ADCMP604BKSZ board (on hand). The drawing calls for the ADCMP600. Output high while the envelope detector output is above the threshold.

ADCMP604 datasheet, ADCMP600 datasheet. Eval board: SMA for IN+ (J1), IN− (J3), IN+FB (J2), IN−FB (J4), OUT+ (J7), OUT− (J8); banana jacks VCC, AGND, CGND/VEE. The back of the board has decoupling capacitors only, no resistors: the inputs are not terminated and there is no 100 Ω across the outputs.

LVDS output: it cannot drive the ADG901 control pin, a 3.3 V FPGA pin or the CGR-201 digital inputs directly. Put 100 Ω across OUT+ and OUT−. To the FPGA: an ECP5 differential input or an LVDS receiver (SN65LVDT2 at 3.3 V has the 100 Ω built in).
Expected behavior
  • VP (IN+) = VENV from the detector, VN (IN−) = threshold. Q high while VENV is above the threshold.
  • Supply 3.3 V: VENV can reach about 2.7 V in the JACON (−27 to +14 dBm at the detector), within VCC + 0.2 V.
  • With almost no hysteresis, noise on VENV near the threshold makes the output toggle several times per pulse. Keep the threshold 10 mV or more above the no-RF VENV, or add positive feedback.
  • Threshold for a given radar level: Envelope detector tab, “Comparator threshold from this curve”. +20 mV trips at −21.5 dBm at the detector.
Test plan

Wiring drawings: envelope_detector/bench_wiring.svg. Supply 3.3 V, 40 mA limit, CGND/VEE tied to AGND.

5Ripple vs thresholdas step 4Pluto CW at TX 0 dB, then TX −10 dBstep IN− up from the no-RF VENV past the CW VENV in the smallest steps available; note B at each stepB solid high, then toggling at ≈400 kHz, then solid low. Width of the toggling band = ripple peak to peak (≈27 mV at TX 0 dB)band ≈±5 % of the VENV rise at both levels
6Edge chatteras step 4, B on the Siglent scope instead (CGR-201 is 5 MHz and misses ns bursts)pulsed, IN− = no-RF + 20 mVzoom on each OUT+ edgea single edgecount extra edges per pulse
For whoever runs the comparator tests: the Pluto puts a ripple on VENV. On 1 Nov, a steady Pluto tone gave a ±13.7 mV, 400 kHz ripple on VENV at TX 0 dB (Envelope detector tab, figure “ripple source and pulse shape”). It comes from a Pluto spur about 25 dB below the tone, not from the detector, so a real radar pulse should not have it. The ADCMP604 has almost no hysteresis (<0.1 mV) and a 1.6 ns delay, so it will follow this ripple wherever the ripple crosses the threshold.
  • Threshold well below the pulse top (no higher than the middle of the VENV rise): the ripple never reaches it, one clean output pulse. This is the normal case.
  • Threshold near the pulse top: the output toggles at 400 kHz during the pulse. Fix: lower the threshold.
  • Pulse only just above the threshold (the weakest detectable level): ripple and noise cross the threshold whatever value is chosen, so the output chatters. The threshold cannot fix this; count it in the S-curve (step 2 of Test C) and plan for the FPGA to ignore “on” periods shorter than a minimum width.
  • Slow Pluto edges (0.65 μs): noise during the rise can give a short burst of toggles at each edge. Ns-scale, so look with the Siglent scope (step 6).
Step 5 measures the ripple with the comparator itself; no separate ripple test is needed first. Unverified: that the ripple is a fixed ≈±5 % of the VENV rise at every level (predicted from the −25 dBc spur, measured only at TX 0 dB; below about −15 dBm it is under the CGR-201’s 5 mV steps). Step 5 at two levels checks it. Moving the Pluto tone offset from 100 kHz to 1 MHz should move the ripple to 4 MHz, which would confirm the source.
Set the CGR-201 output to DC before connecting it: it can swing to −3 V and the comparator input limit is −0.5 V. The 1 kΩ limits the current if it does.

Expected behavior
  • Frequency rises with tuning voltage. The drawing expects 1.0–1.2 GHz for about 6 to 9.5 V.
  • Output about +6 dBm, steady across the band.
  • It should follow a change in tuning voltage in well under the 0.7 µs reply time.
Test plan
  1. Frequency vs tuning voltage, by hand, 0 to 10 V. Done 4 Oct.
  2. Output power vs frequency. Done 6 Oct.
  3. Frequency vs tuning voltage by computer, 0 to 3.5 V in 0.02 V steps. Done 10 Oct.
  4. Response to a voltage step. Done 10 Oct, limited by the 145 ns edge of the Syscomp.
  5. Drift over 74 minutes. Done 10 Oct.
  6. Not done: the computer-run sweep over 4.8 to 7.8 V. The Syscomp stops at 3.52 V. See Tests to run, TX1.

Frequency vs voltage, 0 to 10 V

Result

  • 1.0 GHz needs 4.83 V. 1.2 GHz needs 7.75 V.
  • The line 0.8 GHz + 60 MHz/V is 48 to 97 MHz higher than the measurement.
  • The two data sets differ by up to 16 MHz at the same voltage. The VCO was connected to different things each time.

How it was made

  1. Grey squares: on 4 Oct the tuning voltage was set by hand with a bench supply. The VCO was connected straight to the spectrum analyzer. The frequency was read after waiting 10 s.
  2. Green line: on 10 Oct the computer set the voltage and read the analyzer, 176 points. The VCO was connected to the tee, splitter and mixer.
  3. The orange band marks 1.0–1.2 GHz. The voltages for the band edges were found by interpolating the grey points.
Frequency vs voltage, 0 to 3.5 V

Result

  • 743.6 MHz at 0 V. 920.0 MHz at 3.50 V.
  • 14 points repeated on the way down agree within 0.10 MHz.

How it was made

  1. The Syscomp output is set to a voltage, with its waveform switched off.
  2. Scope CH1 reads the voltage. The Syscomp is adjusted until CH1 is within 3 mV of the target.
  3. The spectrum analyzer does one sweep over 600–1100 MHz and finds the peak.
  4. It does a second sweep 2 MHz wide centred on that peak and reads the peak frequency and power. The marker step is 2 MHz / 751 = 2.7 kHz.
  5. The voltage is raised 0.02 V and the steps repeat. 176 voltages in total.
  6. Then 14 voltages are measured again going down, to check repeatability.
\[ c_{n+1} = c_n + \frac{V_\text{target} - V_\text{CH1}}{1.875\ \text{mV per code}} \]
Code
def set_vt(g, s, target, code):
    s.write(f"C1:OFST {-target:.3f}V")      # centre scope CH1 on the target
    for _ in range(4):
        g.set_offset_raw(code)              # Syscomp output code
        time.sleep(0.6)
        v, _ = scope_mean(s, 1, n=2)        # read Vt on the scope
        if abs(v - target) < 0.003:
            break
        code += (target - v) / OFFSET_V_PER_CODE   # 1.875 mV per code
    return v, code

def measure(self):                          # spectrum analyzer
    f, _ = self._peak(850e6, 500e6)         # wide span: find the peak
    f, p = self._peak(f, 2e6)               # 2 MHz span: read it
    return f, p

Data file: phase_detector_calibration_run3_cleanDC_0p02V_steps.csv. Table: see the Look up tables tab.

Output power vs frequency

Result

  • +7.4 dBm at 1.04 GHz. +4.8 dBm at 1.18 GHz. +4.5 dBm at 1.24 GHz.

How it was made

  1. 6 Oct. VCO connected to the spectrum analyzer through one cable.
  2. The tuning voltage was set by hand to ten values.
  3. Frequency and peak power were read from the analyzer at each.
Analyzer power reading, 744 to 920 MHz

Result

  • 15 of 648 readings were more than 2 dB below the median for their voltage. They occurred at random voltages and times.
  • During those readings the mixer output changed by 0.23 mV at most. The mixer output changes strongly with power. So the VCO power did not really drop.
  • From 850 to 890 MHz the reading is 4 to 7 dB low in every pass.
  • Correlation between the power reading and the VCO tuning slope: −0.89.

Explanation (not tested)

The peak was read through a 30 kHz filter. Noise on the tuning voltage moves the VCO frequency. If it moves by more than 30 kHz during the sweep, part of the signal falls outside the filter and the peak reads low. This is worst where the tuning slope is steepest.

\[ \Delta f_\text{rms} = K_v \cdot \sigma_{V_t} \qquad K_v = 33\ \text{to}\ 90\ \text{MHz/V} \]

With 1 mV of noise this is 33 to 90 kHz. To check: repeat with a 1 MHz filter and averaging.

How it was made

  1. First plot: the peak power from the 2 MHz sweep in the calibration run. One reading per voltage.
  2. Second plot: the same reading taken in each of the 18 drift passes. Dots are the mean. Bars run from the lowest to the highest reading.
Drift over 74 minutes

Result

  • Left panel, VCO frequency: 59 kHz rms scatter. Largest single deviation 324 kHz. No trend with time.
  • The scatter is larger above 2 V. The tuning slope is steeper there, so a 1 mV error in setting the voltage changes the frequency more. The voltage setting repeats to 1.7 mV.

How it was made

  1. The 0 to 3.5 V sweep was run 18 times in a row, in 0.1 V steps (36 voltages). This took 74 minutes.
  2. For each voltage, the median of its 18 readings was calculated.
  3. Each cell is one reading minus the median for that voltage. Red is above the median, blue is below.
  4. Time runs left to right. Voltage runs bottom to top.
\[ \Delta_{ij} = x_{ij} - \operatorname{median}_i(x_{ij}) \]
Code
F = np.array([p["vco_freq_hz"] for p in passes]) / 1e6      # 18 passes x 36 voltages
dF = (F - np.median(F, axis=0)) * 1e3                        # kHz away from the median of that voltage
ax.pcolormesh(minutes, vt, dF.T, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-lim, vmax=lim)
Response to a voltage step, VCO alone

Result

  • Frequency 10–90 % rise time: 100 to 176 ns. The drive voltage rise time is 145 ns.
  • The frequency follows the drive voltage with 0 to 12 ns of lag. The measurement is limited by the drive, not the VCO.
  • The “static DC” curve in the third plot is wrong by up to 1.7 MHz. See the Errors tab.

How it was made

  1. The VCO output was connected to the scope. The mixer was not used.
  2. The scope samples at 500 MSa/s. A 765–875 MHz signal appears in the samples as a lower frequency, 235–125 MHz. This lower frequency is called the alias.
  3. The alias moves by 1 MHz when the real frequency moves by 1 MHz. So the real frequency is 1000 MHz minus the alias.
  4. The Syscomp drove a 50 kHz square wave from 0.5 V to a high level. Ten high levels from 0.75 to 3.0 V.
  5. The signal at the scope was tens of microvolts, smaller than the scope noise. One edge is not enough to see it.
  6. The VCO phase is different on every edge, so the waveforms cannot be averaged directly. Instead, each waveform is multiplied by a copy of itself a few samples earlier. The phase cancels in this product and the frequency remains.
  7. The product was averaged over 1112 edges per step. The angle of the average gives the alias frequency at each instant.
  8. Rise time is the time for the frequency to go from 10 % to 90 % of the step.
\[ f_\text{alias} = |f - k f_s| \qquad f = 2 f_s - f_\text{alias} \quad (750\text{-}1000\ \text{MHz},\ f_s = 500\ \text{MSa/s}) \]
\[ p[n] = z[n+m]\, z^{*}[n] \qquad f_\text{alias} = \frac{f_s}{2\pi m}\arg\langle p[n] \rangle_\text{edges} \]
Code
z = np.fft.ifft(2 * spec * w)                 # keep only the alias band, positive frequencies
p = z[lag:] * np.conj(z[:-lag])               # product of the signal with itself, lag samples earlier
# average p over all edges, then:
f_alias = band_start + np.mod(np.angle(p_avg * np.exp(-2j*np.pi*band_start*lag/fs)), 2*np.pi) * fs / (2*np.pi*lag)
f_true = 1000e6 - f_alias                     # for 750-1000 MHz sampled at 500 MSa/s
Notes

Measured

  • The tuning curve is not a straight line. Use the look up table.
  • The frequency depends on what the output is connected to. Calibrate in the final wiring.
  • The 4 Oct note that the VCO looked slow (seconds) was the bench supply and the analyzer sweep. The VCO responds in under 0.2 µs.
  • The 4 Oct note of two discrete frequency values within 3 MHz was the analyzer marker step (2.67 MHz at a 2 GHz span).

Consequences

  • 1.0–1.2 GHz needs 4.8–7.8 V. The Syscomp reaches 3.52 V. All computer-run tests so far were at 744–920 MHz.
  • Racon tolerance ±1.5 to ±3.5 MHz at 68 MHz/V is ±22 to ±51 mV on the tuning pin.

Not known

  • Change with temperature and supply voltage.
  • Response above 7 MHz. This needs a faster edge than the Syscomp gives.

ADI wiki. The team notes give a maximum output of +11 dBm. The measured output at attenuation 0 dB is about 0 dBm at tone scale 0.5 and +4.7 dBm at tone scale 1.0 (1100 MHz).

Settings found on this unit: sample rate 30.72 MS/s, RF bandwidth 18 MHz. It dropped off USB once during the first run (21:26, 12 Oct) and needed the USB cable replugged.

How the computer controls it

  • Address ip:192.168.2.1 over USB. Program iio_attr.exe. Script clinic\claude\sdr\pluto_cw.py.
  • The tone is made inside the Pluto, 1 MHz above the LO. The LO is set to the wanted frequency minus 1 MHz.
  • Level is set two ways: the attenuation setting (0 to 89.75 dB) and the tone scale (0 to 1, a digital amplitude).
  • pluto_cw.py refuses any attenuation below 31 dB unless the limit is changed in the file. 31 dB keeps the output under −20 dBm. For this test the limit was set to 0 dB, because only the spectrum analyzer (safe to +30 dBm) was connected. It was set back to 31 dB afterwards.
Expected behavior
  • Output falls 1 dB for each 1 dB of attenuation setting.
  • Output changes by 20 log10 of the tone scale.
  • Output is flat within a few dB from 325 MHz to 2.1 GHz.
  • Frequency is within 25 ppm: 27.5 kHz at 1.1 GHz.
  • Besides the tone there is a line at the LO (1 MHz below) and one at the other sideband (2 MHz below). Their levels are not specified.
  • A harmonic at twice the tone frequency. Level not specified.
\[ P_\text{out} = P_0(f) - A + 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{s}{0.5}\right) \]

\(P_0(f)\) = output at attenuation 0 dB and tone scale 0.5. \(A\) = attenuation setting in dB. \(s\) = tone scale.

Test plan

One wiring for every test: Pluto TX to the spectrum analyzer input. Pluto on USB. No wiring changes.
