Results

What was learned

SubjectFindingWhat to do
Highest outputTone scale 1.0, attenuation 0 dB: 6.7 dBm at 400 MHz, 5.7 dBm at 1000 MHz, 4.7 dBm at 1100 MHz, 5.1 dBm at 1200 MHz, 1.5 dBm at 2000 MHz. The team notes say +11 dBm; this unit does not reach it.Plan tests around +5 dBm at most. Add an amplifier if a part needs more.
Level against attenuation settingFollows the setting within 0.6 dB from 20 dB down to 89.75 dB (−89.5 dBm at 1100 MHz). Reads 0.6 to 1.0 dB low at 0 dB.Use the look up table for 0 to 20 dB. From 20 dB up, output = (20 dB reading) + 20 − setting.
0.25 dB stepsAverage step 0.24 dB, but single steps range from 0.09 to 0.41 dB. The same setting gives the same level from above or below (within 0.02 dB).Do not count steps to set a level. Read the level, or use whole-dB settings from the table.
Tone scaleFollows 20 log10(scale) within 0.25 dB at 20 dB attenuation, from scale 0.02 to 1.0.Use the scale as a fine level control when the attenuation is 20 dB or more.
Distortion at high scaleAt scale 1.0 and 0 dB attenuation a line 4 MHz below the tone is only 31 dB under it. At scale 0.5 it is 46 dB under; at scale 0.3, 52 dB under.Keep the tone scale at 0.3 or below when a clean tone matters.
Third harmonic of the LOA line near three times the tone frequency, 10 to 16 dB under the tone. Measured for tones of 350 to 700 MHz. For a 1.0 to 1.2 GHz tone it is at 3.0 to 3.6 GHz, above the spectrum analyzer's range, so not measured there.Assume it is present at 1.0 to 1.2 GHz. Parts that work at 3 GHz (the amplifiers, mixers) receive it. Add a low-pass filter after the Pluto for compression or harmonic tests, and check with the SM200B.
Second and third harmonic of the tone50 to 60 dB under the tone at scale 0.5, 0 dB attenuation. 40 to 60 dB under at scale 1.0.Small enough to ignore next to the line above.
LO leakage and other sidebandAt 1100 MHz, 0 dB attenuation: LO leakage 61 to 67 dB under the tone, other sideband 67 to 72 dB under.No action needed.
Tone offset from the LOLevel is flat within 0.4 dB out to 8 MHz from the LO, 1.3 dB down at 10 MHz, 7.8 dB down at 14 MHz.Keep the tone within 8 MHz of the LO. The scripts use 1 MHz.
Two tonesAt 0 dB attenuation with each tone at scale 0.5, the third-order products are 30 dB under the tones. At 5 dB attenuation with each tone at scale 0.25 to 0.5 they are over 50 dB under.For two-tone tests use 5 dB attenuation or more and each tone at scale 0.4 or less.
Frequency12.6 to 13.1 ppm low against the spectrum analyzer, the same at every frequency.Set the Pluto 12.8 ppm high (14.1 kHz at 1100 MHz) to land on a wanted frequency.
RepeatabilityLeaving 1100 MHz and returning 30 times: level spread 0.03 dB. Setting 0 dB 30 times: 0.01 dB.One reading is enough.
SettlingAfter a retune or an attenuation change the level is at its final value within one 5.3 ms sample.A 0.1 s wait after each change is ample.
FlatnessAt 0 dB: +1.2 dBm at 350 MHz falling to −6.3 dBm near 1600 MHz. 1.1 dB spread inside 1.0 to 1.2 GHz.Use the per-frequency table, not one number, when a test covers more than one frequency. Part of the dip near 1600 MHz moved when the cable was disturbed on 13 Oct, so it is at least partly the cable.
USB, first dropoutDropped off USB at 21:26 on 12 Oct, 5 minutes into the first run. Needed the cable replugged.Scripts should save each reading as it is taken and be able to resume.
LO leakage at low levelsThe LO leakage is about −60 dBm at 0 and 10 dB attenuation whatever the tone scale, −68 dBm at 20 dB, −78 dBm at 30 and 40 dB, then falls 1 dB per dB. With a small tone scale it is close to the tone: at 0 dB attenuation and scale 0.02 the tone is −28 dBm and the LO leakage only 31 dB under it.To get a low level, raise the attenuation and keep the tone scale at 0.2 to 0.5. Do not use a small tone scale at low attenuation.
IF band table1000 to 1200 MHz in 1 MHz steps, attenuation 0 to 40 dB in 2 dB steps (4221 readings). At 0 dB the output is −1.14 to 0.28 dBm. It changes by at most 0.09 dB from one MHz to the next.Use pluto_if_band_table.csv to turn a setting into dBm for any IF-band test.
Tuning stepA request for 5 Hz more moves the tone by about 5 to 7 Hz; 1 kHz more moves it 1001 Hz. During the test the tone was also drifting by 2 to 8 Hz per second.Frequency can be set to a few Hz. Drift, not step size, limits how well the frequency is known.
Noise close to the tone30 to 45 kHz from the tone the noise is about −96 dBc/Hz, and 300 to 450 kHz away about −107 dBc/Hz. One pair of lines 1.4 kHz either side of the 1000 MHz tone, 59 dB under it; none at 1100 or 1200 MHz.This is near what the spectrum analyzer itself contributes, so the Pluto is at least this good. It is not a limit for the planned tests.
Pulsed outputWorks. Level during a pulse equals the continuous-tone level. Width and spacing are correct for pulses from 100 µs down to 300 ns (checked from the spectrum nulls). Below about 100 ns the pulse comes out wider and lower than asked, because the RF bandwidth setting is 18 MHz. Between pulses only the LO leakage remains (about 60 dB under the pulse at 0 dB attenuation).Use sdr\pluto_pulse.py for pulse tests of 300 ns and longer. For 50 ns pulses the sample rate and bandwidth must be raised and rechecked. The spectrum analyzer cannot show pulse shape under 10 µs; use a detector and the oscilloscope.
Warm-upTwo cold starts were logged. From 27 °C the level fell 0.11 dB in 28 minutes. From 25 °C it fell 0.20 dB in 34 minutes and was still falling slowly at 31.6 °C. Frequency error went from about −10.3 ppm cold to −12.4 ppm after 35 minutes and −12.6 ppm after 2 hours.Let it run 45 minutes before a level-critical test and an hour before a frequency-critical one. A cold Pluto reads up to 0.4 dB higher than the tables, which were taken warm (33 °C).
The RF connectionOn 13 Oct after replugging, every level read 0.3 to 0.5 dB higher than the night before, and 1 to 3.5 dB higher from 1250 to 1750 MHz. At 11:31 the computer was moved; the level stepped down 0.45 dB and the whole table then matched the night before within 0.06 dB below 1400 MHz. The Pluto had not changed. The cable or a connector had.Tighten the SMA connectors and do not move the cable during a test. Take the without-part reference with the same cable, in the same position, on the same day. The dip near 1450 to 1700 MHz in the frequency sweep may be the cable, not the Pluto.
Look up functionsdr\pluto_level.py: pluto_dbm(freq, att, scale) gives the output in dBm from the measured 1.0 to 1.2 GHz table; pluto_setting(freq, want_dbm) gives the attenuation setting for a wanted level.Use it to turn settings into power when analysing a chain test. Good to about 0.5 dB across days.
Not measuredPulse rise time (the spectrum analyzer cannot resolve under 10 µs). The line near 3 × LO for 1.0 to 1.2 GHz tones (3.0 to 3.6 GHz is above the analyzer's range).Rise time: a detector on the oscilloscope, or the SM200B. 3 × LO: the SM200B.
USB, second dropoutDropped off USB a second time at 23:51 on 12 Oct, after 2 h 20 min of continuous use. Both times it stopped answering during a frequency change and then disappeared from Windows.Any long run needs someone able to replug it, or a powered USB hub that can be switched from the computer.

Test A: output against attenuation setting, 12 Oct

  1. Wiring: Pluto TX to the spectrum analyzer (Siglent SSA3021X) input. Nothing else connected.
  2. Pluto: one tone, 1 MHz above the LO, tone scale 0.5. The attenuation setting was stepped 0 to 40 dB in 1 dB steps, then 45 to 70 dB in 5 dB steps.
  3. Analyzer: reference level +10 dBm, span 2 MHz centred on the tone, one sweep per reading, peak marker.
  4. Repeated at 1000, 1100 and 1200 MHz. 47 settings at each, 141 readings.

The table above is the measured level minus a straight line of 1 dB per dB drawn through the 20 dB reading.

\[ \text{departure}(A) = P(A) - \left[P(20) + 20 - A\right] \]
  • From 20 to 40 dB the output follows the setting within 0.2 dB.
  • Below 20 dB the output is lower than the setting says: 0.3 to 0.5 dB low at 10 dB, 0.6 to 1.0 dB low at 0 dB. There is a step of about 0.2 dB between 19 and 20 dB.
  • Test G: the analyzer reads the same tone within 0.08 dB at reference levels from −10 to +20 dBm, so the analyzer is not the cause.
  • Test C: at 0 dB the output rises 0.2 dB less than it should between tone scale 0.05 and 0.5. So about 0.2 dB of the shortfall is the output stage compressing. The rest is the attenuator steps not being exact.
  • At 55 dB and above the reading stops falling. The tone is then at the analyzer noise level for this reference level (about −58 dBm). The rows at 55 to 70 dB are not valid Pluto levels.
  • The output at 0 dB and tone scale 0.5 is about 0 dBm (1 mW). At tone scale 1.0 it is +4.7 dBm (3.0 mW) at 1100 MHz. The team notes give a maximum of +11 dBm; this Pluto does not reach that.

Test F: stability

  • 40 readings over 139 s at 1100 MHz, attenuation 20 dB.
  • Level: mean −19.37 dBm, spread 0.03 dB, standard deviation 0.007 dB.

Test E: spectrum

  • At attenuation 0 dB no line stands out of the analyzer noise within 5 MHz of the tone. The LO leakage (1 MHz below) and the other sideband (2 MHz below) are both under −54 dB relative to the tone.
  • At attenuation 20 dB the analyzer noise is only 36 dB under the tone with these settings, so that trace gives no better limit.
  • From 30 MHz to 2.1 GHz at attenuation 0 dB, nothing else is above the noise, 45 dB under the tone.
  • These are limits set by the analyzer settings (reference level +10 dBm, automatic bandwidth). The overnight run repeats this with a narrower bandwidth to find the actual levels.

Second harmonic of the 1000 MHz tone, read at 2000 MHz: −57.50 dBm at attenuation 20 dB; −49.08 dBm at attenuation 0 dB.

Files

Folder clinic\claude\pluto_characterization\: readings.csv (every reading, with time, settings, measured frequency and level), characterize_pluto.py (takes the readings), analyze_pluto.py (tables and plots), summary.json, pluto_tx_calibration.csv, spectrum_*.csv (traces, test E), run_log.txt.

Overnight run, 12 to 13 Oct

Started 21:44 on 12 Oct. Same wiring: Pluto TX straight into the spectrum analyzer. 11643 readings and 227 saved traces so far (last reading 2026-10-13 16:08:08). Script overnight.py, readings overnight_readings.csv, traces in traces\, analysis analyze_overnight.py, numbers overnight_summary.json.

Low level: output down to the 89.75 dB setting

  1. One analyzer setting cannot cover 0 to −90 dBm. Four were used: reference level +10 dBm; −10 dBm; −30 dBm with the preamp, 1 kHz bandwidth; the same with 100 Hz bandwidth.
  2. Each setting was read at five attenuation settings shared with the one before. The average difference over those five is the correction that ties it to the one before.
  3. The +10 dBm setting is used for 0 to 40 dB, the −10 dBm setting to 60 dB, the preamp settings above that.
\[ c_2 = \overline{P_1(A) - P_2(A)}\ \text{over the shared}\ A \qquad P(A) = P_2(A) + c_2 \]

\[ f_\text{IM3} = 2f_1 - f_2 \quad\text{and}\quad 2f_2 - f_1 \]

At 0 dB attenuation the products grow fast with scale (60 dB under at scale 0.1, 30 dB under at scale 0.5). At 5 dB attenuation and scale 0.5 they are 53 dB under. The output stage is the cause.

Settling

  • Analyzer at 1100 MHz with zero span: it records level against time, one point every 5.3 ms, bandwidth 300 kHz.
  • Left: the Pluto was moved from 900 to 1100 MHz. Right: attenuation changed from 40 to 20 dB. Six repeats each.
  • In every repeat the level is within 0.5 dB of its final value at the first point after the change. Settling takes less than one point.
  • The delay between sending the command over USB and the change appearing was not measured.

  2. The first and last rows of each set both ask for +0 Hz. The tone had moved between them: 56 Hz in 23 s at 1000 MHz; 184 Hz in 23 s at 1100 MHz.
  3. That drift is taken as a straight line in time and subtracted in the last column.

With the drift removed the tone follows requests of 50 Hz and more within about 10 Hz at 1000 MHz. The 1100 MHz set drifted faster and is less clear. The LO setting has a resolution of a few Hz; drift is the larger effect.

Pulsed output, 13 Oct

Script sdr\pluto_pulse.py. The Pluto is sent a repeating block of samples: a constant value for the pulse, zeros between pulses. The RF is at the LO frequency during the pulse. Sample rate 30.72 MS/s, so the width is a whole number of 32.55 ns samples. Same wiring: Pluto TX straight into the spectrum analyzer. 1100 MHz.

  • The pulse level matches the continuous tone within 0.2 dB where both were read in the same hour (amplitude 0.5). The amplitude 1.0 tone values are from the night before; that morning every level read 0.3 to 0.5 dB higher because of the RF connection (see below).
  • Between pulses the reading is −54.6 to −55.7 dBm, which is the analyzer's noise in this bandwidth. The pulse is at least 55 dB above it. The LO leakage (about −60 dBm at 0 dB attenuation, from the continuous-tone tests) is still there between pulses, so the true on/off ratio at 0 dB attenuation is about 60 dB.

  1. One pulse every 100 µs, attenuation 0 dB, amplitude 0.5. Analyzer: 100 kHz bandwidth, positive-peak detector, 3 s sweep, so each point of the trace sees about 40 pulses and keeps the largest.
  2. A first attempt with a normal fast sweep gave a ragged trace (each point either caught a pulse or missed it). Those traces are saved as pulse_spectrum_* and are not used.
  3. The spectrum of a rectangular pulse of width τ has nulls at multiples of 1/τ from the centre. The null positions were found from the trace and compared with 1/τ.
  4. In a bandwidth narrower than 1/τ the peak reading falls 20 dB for each tenfold drop in width. The departure column is the reading minus that rule, taking the 1000 ns pulse as the reference.
\[ \Delta f_\text{null} = \frac{1}{\tau} \qquad P_\text{peak}(\tau) = P_\text{peak}(\tau_0) + 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\tau}{\tau_0}\right) \]
  • The 5000 ns pulse is wider than the analyzer filter can treat as short, so the 20 log rule does not apply to it.
  • From 2000 ns down to 300 ns the nulls are where 1/τ says and the peak follows the 20 log rule within 0.3 dB. The Pluto makes these pulses with the right width and full amplitude.
  • For 200 ns the first null (5.1 MHz expected) can be seen in the plot near 5 MHz.
  • Below about 130 ns the departure grows (+0.9 dB at 130 ns, +1.5 dB at 65 ns, +4.3 dB at one sample). The spectrum is cut off beyond about ±10 MHz: the Pluto's RF bandwidth setting is 18 MHz. A pulse shorter than about 100 ns comes out wider and lower than asked.
  • To make the 50 ns pulses the design calls for, the Pluto's sample rate and RF bandwidth would have to be raised. That has not been tried and would need its own check.
  • After each pulse test the normal tone generator was switched back on and read: −18.82 and −18.99 dBm at 20 dB, as before.

Readings that are not used

Power readings by test: 50 Ω load vs antenna, every chain

Peak at the SM200B (3 MHz RBW, Min/Max, Max Hold). Blue: 50 Ω load on the SM200B. Orange: load → 29 dB pads. Green: Vivaldi → 29 dB pads. Made by radar_test/plot_load_vs_antenna.py.

A. 50 Ω load, no antenna: what leaks in

A load cannot receive, so these readings are radar power that gets into the SM200B, its cables and the pads directly. Every antenna reading has to be at least 20 dB above the load reading for the same wiring and distance.

Load directly on the SM200B input (13 ft)
Test 17 · 25 Oct 16:55 · 3.96 m (13 ft) · 50 Ω load directly on the SM200B input (no pads) · foam off — SM200B: −15.7 dBm (Spike) → no source in the chain; this is radar leaking straight into the SM200B, cables and pads

Sorin's notes

  • “terminator is on the signal hound input now, no pads. Just 50 ohm term to a line to the signal hound” (16:54).

Setup

  • The 29 dB of pads removed; the 50 Ω termination screwed straight onto the SM200B input. No cable.
AI analysis
  • 5 dB more than the load through 29 dB of pads (test 16) a few minutes earlier: adding 29 dB took off only 5 dB, so most of the leak enters the SM200B itself, not through its input.
  • Same wiring as test 21 the next day (−22.5 dBm); the 7 dB difference is the radar and SM200B not being in exactly the same places and the cables around them.
  • SM200B safety: 35 dB under its +20 dBm limit.

AI analysis
  • 6 dB more than without the board (test 22). The board is not transmitting: it reflects. In a room, a metal sheet sends energy round its edges and off the walls, and the 2.6 s rotation means the beam sweeps across many paths. A sheet only shadows well when it is much bigger than the beam and nothing reflects behind it.

Attenuator pads on the VNA: the 3, 6 and 10 dB “8G” pads

Agilent 8720ES, 85052D kit (3.5 mm), full 2-port cal: 50 MHz–20.05 GHz, 801 points, IF BW 1 kHz, −10 dBm. Cal REG26 was made with the first cable; recalibrated with the better cable for the sweeps below. All values in dB. Copy-paste version: radar_test/vna/pad_measurements.csv. 3 dB pad, sweep 3 (marker readings, better cable, recalibrated; use these):

FrequencyS21 (loss)S12S11 (in match)S22 (out match)
50 MHz−2.943 dB−2.932 dB−49.61 dB−48.01 dB

10.000 GHz−3.564 dB−3.749 dB−16.46 dB−16.68 dB

  • At 9.4 GHz the “3 dB” pad loses 3.6–3.9 dB, about 0.6–0.9 dB more than its label. It is rated only to 8 GHz.
  • S21 and S12 differ by 0.33 dB at 9.4 GHz. A passive pad is reciprocal, so that difference is measurement error, and it sets the uncertainty of these numbers.
  • The cable mattered: the same pad read 4.18 dB at 9.5 GHz on the first cable (sweep 2) and 3.6 dB at 9.4 GHz on this one.
  • Sweep 1 showed an S21 notch to −10 dB and an S22 spike to ~0 dB near 5.7 GHz. That is more power out than in (|S21|² + |S22|² > 1), so it was not the pad; it is gone in sweeps 2 and 3. Sweep 1 readings were by eye and are superseded.

Test log: all tests as one table (25 and 26 Oct)

Every test run on 25 and 26 Oct 2026, in order. Repeated readings of one setup are one test (old 5 and 6 are in 4, 14 in 13, 19 in 20); numbers were not reused. Readings are the peak at the SM200B input unless stated.

Times are Pacific (UTC−7), taken from the time stamps of Sorin's messages; "≈" means worked out from the messages around it.

"Sorin" = Sorin read it or said it; "Spike" = Claude read a Spike screenshot; "I/Q" = Claude's own Python capture.

The same tests grouped by wiring, with Sorin's exact words: Radar tab → "Power readings by test".

"3 MHz" means Spike or I/Q at a bandwidth wide enough to hold the 0.68 µs pulse (close to the true pulse peak);

"100 kHz" readings are 15 to 25 dB lower than the true peak for this pulse.

Radar: Furuno 1722C, long pulse (24 nm range), 2.2 kW peak rating. Supply 12 V 4.64 A on standby (Sorin, 11:59), 12.15 V 4.5 A setting (Sorin, 13:38), 12.1 V 6.35 A transmitting.

Distances are radar to Vivaldi. 11.3 m = 37 ft (Sorin); on 26 Oct Sorin gave the same spot as 11 to 11.5 m. "Pads" are the fixed 8 GHz attenuators in front of the SM200B.

What the tests show

  1. Radar signal (test 4): fully characterized; leakage does not change these figures.
  2. SM200B safety: the highest reading in any test was −7.94 dBm (test 27), 28 dB under the +20 dBm limit.
  3. Leakage (tests 9, 15–24): the radar gets into the SM200B directly at about −20 to −25 dBm at 13 ft. Power levels in tests 8–18 are mixed with it and are not reliable as antenna levels; test 7 is 11 dB above the 11.5 m floor and mostly signal.
  4. Limiter: the 0.8 dB loss from tests 11–12 was measured at the leak floor (test 25b) and is not trustworthy. Output +16.2 dBm at 13 ft (test 13), within its rated clamping level, but the input level for that test is not known, so clamping is not yet shown.
  5. Leak floor at 11.5 m (tests 25–26): −31 dBm with a load on the pads, whiteboard in or out; −28 dBm with the LNA powered and a load on the limiter input; −24 dBm with 20 dB before and 19 dB after the LNA.
  6. LNA (tests 27–28): Vivaldi → limiter → 20 dB → LNA → 19 dB read −7.94 dBm with the LNA on, 16 dB above the floor, and −25.85 dBm with it off. With the LNA input estimated from test 7 (about −12 dBm), the gain is about 23 dB (datasheet about 22). The on/off difference (17.9 dB) is limited by the leak.

Lessons

  • The JFW manual attenuator is rated DC–2.5 GHz and does almost nothing at 9.4 GHz.
  • Spike's Average detector reads far below a radar pulse peak; use Min/Max, Log, 3 MHz RBW, Max Hold.
  • Spike resets to defaults after every SM200B reconnect; check settings each time.
  • Only one Spike window at a time.
  • Repeat the load test at the start of every setup: the leak must be 20 dB below the reading being trusted.

Spike screens, 26 Oct at 11.5 m (3 MHz RBW, Min/Max, Max Hold)

Test 25b: 50 Ω load → 29 dB pads, whiteboard out. The leak floor: −31.2 dBm.

Test 27: Vivaldi → limiter → 20 dB → LNA on → 19 dB. −7.94 dBm, 16 dB above the −24.06 dBm floor of the same chain with a load (26c).

Test 28: same, LNA off. −25.85 dBm.

Test 29 (31 Oct): same wiring as test 28 (Vivaldi → limiter → 10+10 → LNA unpowered → 10+6+3; Sorin had not turned on the amp power). −19.12 dBm at 9.408594 GHz, 6.7 dB above test 28 and 4.9 dB above the floor of this chain.

Test 30 (31 Oct): limiter → 20 dB → LNA powered on → 10+6+3+10 (29 dB). −32.83 dBm at 9.40625 GHz, about 15 dB below the −18 dBm expected from test 27 plus 10 dB. Scaled to 19 dB after the LNA it is 3.7 dB below test 29 with the LNA off, so the LNA shows no gain here. Cause not known.

Test 30b: same wiring, ref −20 dBm. Peak about −33 dBm by eye (marker was off the peak), the same as test 30. The floor drops about 30 dB, to about −82 dBm, which shows the skirts that ref +10 hid.

Test 31: same wiring, RBW 100 kHz. −49.46 dBm at 9.405664 GHz (Max Hold). Sorin saw the 6 V supply move it only from −54 to −52 dBm, where tests 27 and 28 differed by 17.9 dB. Either the LNA is not amplifying or this signal bypasses it. Sinc lobes are about 1.5 MHz apart by eye, about a 0.65 µs pulse.

Test 32: 50 Ω load directly on the limiter input instead of the antenna (which had been on a meter of cable), LNA on at 0.08 A. −23.15 dBm at 3 MHz RBW and −45.04 dBm at 100 kHz RBW, both at 9.40625 GHz. The load reads higher than the antenna by 9.7 and 4.4 dB, so tests 30 and 31 are leak, not signal through the chain. They do not show the LNA gain. Why the antenna path gave well under the expected −18 dBm is not known.

Test 33: Vivaldi directly on the limiter, no meter of cable. −18.94 dBm at 9.405469 GHz, 3 MHz RBW, near the expected −18 dBm. That is 13.9 dB above test 30 with the cable, which points at that cable or its connection, and only 4.2 dB above the load reading in test 32. The peak is above the −20 dBm ref, so it may read low; to be rechecked at a higher ref.

Test 34: Vivaldi → limiter → 20 dB → LNA → 29 dB → SM200B, no PLL or mixer. Sorin read −16.46 dBm with the amp on and −27.39 dBm with the amp off, 10.93 dB apart, which is a lower bound on the gain. No screenshot; Spike settings not stated.

Test 35, radar off, baseline for the mix-down: Vivaldi → limiter → 20 dB → LNA → 6+10 → ZX05-14LH-S+ RF; ADF 8.3 GHz → buffer → ZX10 → mixer LO; IF → 3 dB → SM200B. LO at the IF port: −30.62 dBm at 8.300002 GHz. By eye, about −32 dBm near 4.15 GHz and −52 dBm near 16.6 GHz.

Test 36, mix-down, same wiring with a radar signal showing: IF about −37.5 dBm near 1.1058 GHz (by eye, RBW 3 MHz), matching 9.4055 − 8.3 = 1.1055 GHz and about 20 dB above the IF floor. RF feedthrough about −39 dBm near 9.4055 GHz (by eye, RBW 200 kHz). LO feedthrough −30.19 dBm at 8.299951 GHz (RBW 100 kHz). Apparent conversion loss about 30 dB, using about −4 dBm RF from test 34, against 7.72 dB in the datasheet at +10 dBm LO; LO here is about −6 dBm. No LO-off control yet.

Test 36b, second look, same wiring, both at RBW 3 MHz: IF −38.57 dBm at 1.105469 GHz and −19.82 dBm at 9.404688 GHz, 18.75 dB apart. The 9.4 GHz reading is close to the test 32 leak (−23.15 dBm), so it is not a clean feedthrough number. Apparent conversion loss about 31.6 dB, using about −4 dBm RF from test 34.

Test 36c, control: with the PLL off, Sorin saw no 1.1 GHz signal, so the peak is the mixing product.

Decisions (Sorin, 31 Oct): the ZX10 splitter stays in the LO path because the transmit up-converter will need the other output. No second LO amp for now, so each mixer gets about −6 dBm of LO, about 16 dB under the +10 dBm spec. Likely cost: the extra conversion loss seen above, not yet proven to be from the LO. The envelope detector reference and the RF limiting amp on the frequency path are set after the mixer. To check: whether about −36 dBm at the mixer IF port clears their input sensitivity, and the transmit output level. Next: measure the IF on the oscilloscope and SSA 3021X, then add the frequency identification.

Test 37: IF to the SDS1104X-E and SSA3021X. SSA at 1.105 GHz, RBW 1 MHz (its maximum): swept 100 MHz span shows no peak (−55.79 dBm max); zero span, atten 0, 30 s Max Hold gives −50.86 dBm max against a −66.06 dBm median. Not yet confirmed as the IF; needs a PLL-off control. The scope trace is flat: the SDS1104X-E is a 1 MΩ, 100 MHz scope, so it cannot show 1.1 GHz.

Test 38: same chain, IF → 3 dB → SM200B, nothing else changed. IF about −37 dBm near 1.104 GHz by eye (RBW 3 MHz, ref −20), agreeing with test 36b. The chain still works, so the weak test 37 reading comes from the scope/SSA path or the SSA’s narrower RBW.

Test 39: IF directly on the SSA3021X, no pad or scope. RBW 1 MHz, atten 0. Zero span at 1.105 GHz: −50.88 and −54.76 dBm max over 30 s. Swept 100 MHz with a 1 s sweep: −61.54 dBm at 1.1056 GHz. The frequency agrees with Spike. The level matches test 37 with the scope in, so the scope was not the loss. It is about 15 dB below the −35.6 dBm Spike implies; the 1 MHz RBW against a 0.65 µs pulse should explain about 9.5 dB, and the rest is not explained. No PLL-off control on the SSA.

Test 39b, retake with radar and PLL on: zero span −54.73 dBm max; swept −58.52 dBm at 1.1031 GHz. The swept peak is sparse spikes because the sweep catches pulses only now and then, so its frequency and level vary between runs. Markers on the screens are not on the peak; the numbers come from the trace data.

Test 40, first look at the phase detector: mixer IF → ZFRSC-42-S+ → two cables, one 4.5 in longer → ZX05-30W-S+ LO and RF; its IF → SDS1104X-E, radar on. Scope flat at its old settings (120 mV/div, 1 ms/div). Not a valid test yet: each detector port gets about −42 dBm (6 dB resistive splitter), about 49 dB under the +7 dBm LO spec, so little or no output is expected until the limiting amp is in. Plan: three ZX60-P103LN+ at 5.0 V (5.5 V absolute max) after the mixer, about 15 dB each at 1.1 GHz by datasheet, giving about +9 dBm before the splitter and +3 dBm at each detector port. At those levels they do not compress (+22.4 dBm output), so they amplify but do not limit.

Test 41 (1 Nov), phase detector calibration with the Pluto as source: Pluto −36 dBm → 3 × ZX60-P103LN+ → ZFRSC-42-S+ → two cables, one 4.5 in longer → ZX05-30W-S+; IF → scope CH1 and SSA3021X. Output is about 187 mV at 1008 MHz, about 250 mV at 1080 MHz, about 235 mV at 1134 MHz, about 244 mV at 1184 MHz, and 243.2 mV at 1105 MHz. It gives one voltage per frequency only from about 1010 to 1080 MHz (about 0.9 mV/MHz); at 1105 MHz the slope is about −0.7 mV/MHz and the same voltage recurs above 1170 MHz. Two runs agree from 1014 MHz up (mean 0.31 mV, max 2.8 mV); run 1 was bad below 1014 MHz, cause not known. With the tone off the output was about 43 mV with 12 mV rms, cause not known; oscillation not ruled out. Data: phase_detector_calibration/pluto_calibration_1nov_-36dBm_run2.csv.

Test 41b: same wiring, 800 to 999 MHz. 191 mV at 800 MHz, falling to 99.4 mV near 886 MHz, rising to about 190 mV near 990 MHz. Steepest long run about 950 to 985 MHz, about 1.6 mV/MHz by eye. The scope input is 1 MΩ (the SDS1104X-E has no 50 Ω setting), so this curve holds only for that load at DC.

Test 42, full chain with the Furuno as source, PLL on: pulses with a flat top near 195 mV (peaks 200 to 204 mV), about 0.8 µs wide, on an 8 to 15 mV baseline. The Pluto curve predicted 243 mV. The scope triggered at 200 mV but not at 250 mV. An earlier PLL-off capture is marked bad by Sorin. The SSA3021X shows up to about −2 dBm near DC, rolling off by about 2 MHz, and nothing clear above its −48 dBm floor up to 2.1 GHz.

Test 43: detector output → 23 dB → SM200B. −68.06 dBm at 1.104688 GHz, about −45 dBm before the pad. Spike was on Power/Average, so a pulsed signal reads low; this is not a peak level.

Test 44: same, raw I/Q at 50 MS/s, PLL on. Before the pad: +3.07 dBm near DC and −15.92 dBm at 1104.27 MHz, so the near-DC pulse is about 19 dB above the leftover 1.1 GHz. Pulse width within 10 dB: 0.74 and 0.64 µs. Pulse spacing about 1650 and 1680 µs. The near-DC capture shows a slow tail after each pulse (about −8 to −14 dBm over 2.5 µs) that the scope did not show; cause not known.

Test 45: same, PLL off deliberately. Before the pad: −7.90 dBm near DC and −29.47 dBm in the 1.105 GHz capture, 11 dB and 13.6 dB below PLL on. The scope did not trigger at any level from 400 down to 100 mV; whether it was still connected was not stated. Some radar output still reaches the detector with the PLL off; path not known. The antenna was hand-held in the same orientation for both. No line at 1105 MHz with the PLL off: the spectrum of the strongest pulse peaks at −73.8 dB at 1111.35 MHz, against −59.4 dB at 1104.27 MHz with the PLL on. In the saved 60 ms the PLL on near DC capture has 37 pulses 1.6 to 1.7 ms apart, while PLL off has no train at that spacing, only 20 to 80 ns spikes (highest −7.9 dBm) with the strongest clusters about 6 ms apart. Weaker spikes of about −14 dBm also appear between pulses with the PLL on, so the PLL does not create them; the cause is unknown, and a radar off capture has not been taken. Test 46 repeated the leak check with the Pluto at 1105 MHz, −36 dBm (table), into the same three amps and detector: −30.2 dBm at 1105 MHz with the tone on and no line above −90 dBm with it off (before the 23 dB pads, which were assumed still in place). So the Pluto leaks too; the calibration read DC on the 100 MHz scope and could not show it. The radar's −15.9 dBm leak is 14 dB higher, though earlier levels put both near +5 dBm at the detector ports; the difference is not explained. Only 60 ms around the strongest pulse was kept, so these captures do not show a full rotation. Data: phase_detector_calibration/furuno_detector_1nov_pll_on and furuno_detector_1nov_pll_off_deliberate.

Spike max-hold exports, 100 kHz and 3 MHz RBW
  • Sorin's exports from Spike: data/Furino Characterization/14db8G_11meters_100khzrbw.csv and 14db8G_11meters_3mhzrbw.csv. Plot made by radar_test/plot_spike_exports.py.
  • Setup: Vivaldi at 11.3 m facing the radar, AN-72 foam on the radar, whiteboard out, 14 dB of 8 GHz pads, manual attenuator at 0 dB.
  • 100 kHz RBW: peak −44.7 dBm at 9403.008 MHz, −3 dB width 1.27 MHz. Sidelobes on the high side at +2.05, +3.47, +5.20, +6.62 MHz: −10.0, −14.6, −17.1, −19.3 dB. Their spacing (about 1.5 MHz) gives a pulse width of about 0.68 µs.
  • 3 MHz RBW: peak −20.5 dBm (9.0 µW) at 9403.594 MHz. This filter is wide enough to hold the pulse, so this is close to the true pulse peak and agrees with the I/Q measurement (−22 dBm).
  • The 24.2 dB difference between the two peaks is the narrow filter missing most of the pulse's energy, not a change in the radar.

Second harmonic, 18.805 GHznot detected; under −41.7 dBm at the SM200B while the fundamental was −22 dBmSo at least 20 dB down in this measurement. The limit is the measurement, not the radar.
Peak power received here−22 dBm at the SM200B; at least −8 dBm at the Vivaldi outputsee the table belowThrough AN-72 foam, at 11.3 m. Cable and manual attenuator loss at 9.4 GHz not yet measured, so the true antenna output is somewhat higher.

\[ P_r = \underbrace{63.4 + 24}_{\text{EIRP, dBm}} + G_r - 20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi d}{\lambda}\right), \qquad \lambda = 3.19\ \text{cm} \]
  • 63.4 dBm = 2.2 kW peak. 24 dBi = the radar antenna gain implied by its 5.2° × 25° beam. Gr = 12.5 dBi for the racon horn.
  • Main beam, line of sight, no foam. These are design values; the measurement here was through foam and is about 30 dB lower than this formula gives for 11.3 m and a 10 dBi antenna.
  • Average power at any distance is 34 dB below the peak in the table.
  • The limiter must take the closest-approach peak (+28 dBm at 10 m) and keep the LNA input under its +15 dBm limit; the limiter's spike leakage on a 20 ns edge is what to check.
One pulse: shape, I and Q, frequency inside the pulse
  • Top left: power, one sample every 20 ns. Half-power width 660 ns.
  • Top right: amplitude. Rise and fall 80 ns between 10 % and 90 % here.
  • Bottom left: I and Q after removing the carrier. Both are smooth through the pulse: the carrier is clean; the slow change in Q is a small frequency offset and drift.
  • Bottom right: the instantaneous frequency across the flat top, within about 1 MHz of the carrier.

The SM200B mixes 9402.6 MHz down to zero inside the instrument and only then samples, so the stored data has no carrier in it: I and Q, 50 million complex samples a second. Nothing here is filtered or shifted by us. Seeing the oscillation itself needs either a scope sampling faster than about 20 GS/s at 9.4 GHz, or the signal mixed down to a frequency the SDS1104X-E can sample. The strongest pulse's 250 samples: radar_test/raw_20261025_130811_strongest_pulse.csv; script radar_test/plot_raw_iq_all.py.

  • Left: the raw I samples as the SM200B gives them, one every 20 ns. The SM200B has already removed the 9.4 GHz carrier, so what is left is the pulse envelope times a slowly turning phase. That phase differs from pulse to pulse, which is why some rows step up and some step down.
  • Right: the same samples moved to a 5 MHz display frequency so the oscillation shows. The real carrier makes about 6,600 cycles in one 0.7 µs pulse; no instrument here can draw them one by one (the SDS1104X-E stops at 100 MHz).
  • Each pulse starts at a different phase of the oscillation: a magnetron starts fresh every pulse, so pulses are not coherent with each other.
  • Peak 22.7 mV at the SM200B input (50 Ω), the strongest pulse at −22.9 dBm. Data: 25 Oct, 13:08, radar_test/raw_20261025_130811.npz. Every sample of every pulse window: radar_test/pulse_wiggles_raw.csv (I and Q in √mW). Script: radar_test/plot_pulse_wiggles.py.

A 0.32 µs sliding FFT through the pulse. One frequency throughout; energy spreads only at the switching edges.

FFT of a pulse, with bandwidth markers
  • Each FFT covers 2 µs around one pulse. Orange: power average of the 23 pulses within 3 dB of the strongest. Dotted: an ideal 660 ns rectangular pulse.
  • Bandwidth 1.30 MHz at −3 dB, 2.20 MHz at −10 dB, 7.8 MHz at −20 dB.
  • The nulls are where the ideal pulse puts them (multiples of 1/660 ns = 1.52 MHz); the sidelobes are uneven, which a small frequency drift inside the pulse causes.
Pulse train and waterfall
  • Top: 60 ms of the strongest beam pass. Purple numbers are the time between pulses in µs.
  • Bottom: one row per pulse, each row that pulse's spectrum. Every pulse is at the same frequency (red dots: mean −0.103 MHz from 9402.6 MHz, 74 kHz standard deviation).
  • The dip in strength in the middle of the pass is the beam's shape plus room reflections.
Time between pulses

Over 9,900 intervals: 16 values from 1606.5 to 1706.5 µs, 6.67 µs apart, used about equally and mixed in a repeating order. A racon cannot predict the next pulse from the last interval.

Rotation and the beam as seen from the Vivaldi
  • Rotation 2.5885 s (23.18 rpm), from 30 s of every pulse with no samples lost.
  • Main beam −22.2 dBm. Half a turn away (−166°) there is a second response 10.6 dB lower: the back of the antenna or a reflection off the room behind the Vivaldi. Other bumps at ±50° and +120° are reflections.
  • The −3 dB width here (16°) is wider than the 5.2° specification because of reflections and the short distance.
Pulse statistics

From 30 s at 50 MS/s: the 152 pulses within 3 dB of the strongest for the edge figures; 705 pulses above −30 dBm for frequency.

Swept spectra, 0 to 20 GHz
  • Swept max hold at several spans, 12 to 30 s each. Nothing found from 5 to 9 GHz, 10.8 to 13 GHz, or near 18.8 GHz above the sweep noise (about −48 to −54 dBm with a 3 MHz RBW).
  • A swept analyzer only catches a pulse when the sweep and the beam line up, so peak levels on these plots read low and differ from scan to scan. Use the I/Q measurements above for power.
Setup and safety
 Furuno 1722C/NT radar, NavNet, 12.1 V 6.35 A          long-range pulse (LP), 24 nm range
 AN-72 absorber foam over the radome face
          ~~~ 11.3 m (37 ft) of air, room with walls ~~~
 Vivaldi R120 antenna (5-13 GHz), facing the radar
          |  long SMA cable
 JFW 50DR-046 manual attenuator, set to 0 dB     (rated DC-2.5 GHz: not counted at 9.4 GHz)
          |
 10 dB fixed attenuator (8 GHz)  +  2 dB (8 GHz)  +  2 dB (8 GHz)   = 14 dB counted
          |
 Signal Hound SM200B, +20 dBm max input, internal attenuator 30 dB, reference level +20 dBm
  • SM200B damage limit +20 dBm. Worst case before the test, with only the 14 dB of fixed pads counted, the radar's main beam on a 10 dBi antenna at 11.3 m: +10.4 dBm at the SM200B, 9.6 dB under the limit.
  • The manual attenuator was not counted: JFW rates it DC to 2.5 GHz. Setting it from 50 dB to 0 dB changed the reading by only about 3 dB, confirming it does little at 9.4 GHz.
  • Changes were made one at a time with a reading between: Vivaldi pointed away (−38.8 dBm in 10 MHz RBW), turned to face the radar, whiteboard removed and manual attenuator to 0 dB (−21.5 dBm in Spike, 3 MHz RBW). Highest pulse peak at the SM200B in all captures: −21.6 dBm, 41.6 dB under the limit.
  • Radar supply: 12.1 V, 6.35 A (77 W) transmitting; 4.64 A in standby. Antenna does not turn in standby.
  • SM200B internal temperature 24 °C at switch-on, 49 °C after an hour; Spike showed 47 to 48 °C.
Files and how the numbers were made
  • Folder radar_test/ in the repository.
  • sm200b_scan.py, sm200b_monitor.py: swept scans and the safety monitor used during setup.
  • radar_pulses.py: I/Q streaming. 50 MS/s (one sample every 20 ns, 41.5 MHz bandwidth) for pulse shape; 6.25 MS/s for 30 s timing captures that keep up with no lost samples. Finds every pulse 15 dB above the noise and records time, peak, width, rise, fall, carrier frequency and chirp. Output folders pulses_*.
  • capture_raw.py: 60 ms of raw I/Q around the strongest beam pass, raw_*.npz.
  • plot_raw.py, plot_stats.py: the plots on this tab, written to radar_test/plots/. radar_spectra.py: the swept spectra.
  • Rotation: autocorrelation of the received power, 1 ms bins, refined over four turns. Beam plot: time folded modulo the rotation period. Carrier frequency: mean phase step between samples on the flat top of each pulse.
  • Power is |I + jQ|² of the SM200B's corrected 32-bit I/Q, which is in mW at its input.

Radar test 25 Oct: spectrum scans (baseline and with the radar on)

Script radar_test/sm200b_monitor.py says:

Continuous watch of 9.0-10.8 GHz on the SM200B while the radar is on. Run from clinic/claude/signal_hound.

    python ../radar_test/sm200b_monitor.py [minutes]

Each line is one 3 s max-hold (longer than one antenna rotation, 2.0-2.5 s): the largest level, where, and the
margin to the +20 dBm limit. Every line is saved to radar_test/monitor_<time>.csv and the last max-hold trace to
radar_test/scans/monitor_last.csv.

RBW is 10 MHz, the widest, so a radar pulse reads close to its true peak. For a 0.8 us pulse the reading is within
about 1 dB of the peak; for a 0.08 us pulse it can read 2 to 6 dB low. The "margin" printed assumes the worse case
and subtracts 6 dB.

Internal attenuator 30 dB, ref level +20 dBm. This watch cannot protect the instrument by itself: the damage would
be done by the first pulse. It tells you how much room there is before you move the antenna or the radar.

Capture the Furuno radar's pulses with the SM200B (I/Q streaming, 50 MS/s, 41.5 MHz bandwidth) and measure:
pulse spacing, pulse width, rise and fall time, peak power, the beam pass profile and the rotation period.

whole capture (envelope_10us.csv), 40 us of raw I/Q around the 20 strongest pulses (snippets.npz), plots, summary.json.

Racon

SeaBeacon 2 racon answering the Furuno 1722C/NT, received over the air with the SM200B on 9 Nov 2026. This is the reply the JACON has to copy: Morse R, its timing, its frequency and its edges. Every plot shows the wiring it was taken with.

Summary

Interactive raw I/Q viewer: the whole 250 MS/s horn recording (every sample of all 2671 snippets; zoom on a selection, pan, step reply by reply, jump to the Furuno pulse).

  • Frequency relative to the Furuno: dash minus Furuno peak +1.95, median 2.09, mean 2.18, sd 3.10 MHz; 5-95 % -2.6 to 7.1 MHz. The racon picks a new frequency for each reply and does not follow the radar from pulse to pulse.
  • Inside a reply it climbs steadily: dot 2 is 0.72 MHz above dot 1 (sd 0.29), a chirp of about 0.029 MHz/us in the dash and faster in dot 1.
  • Morse R (dot dash dot) after every radar pulse it hears. 7324 long and 1601 short complete replies measured.
  • Two versions. Long R: dot 8.51 us, gap 8.57 us, dash 25.65 us, whole reply 59.83 us. Short R: everything about 0.75 times as long (dot 6.35, gap 6.42, dash 19.19, whole 44.77 us). About one reply in five is short; the short ones come in one block per pass of the radar beam (see below).
  • Timing is crystal-steady. Long R gaps and dash vary by about 0.059 and 0.077 us (1 sd), a few nanoseconds once the rare faded replies are left out (see the histograms).
  • Delay jitters. Dot 1 starts 1.72 us after the radar pulse starts (long R; 5-95 % 1.39 to 2.45 us). Short R start earlier and steadier (1.34 us).
  • Edges are fast: about 30 ns 10-90 % at 250 MS/s (160 MHz bandwidth), close to what the SM200B itself can show. The radar pulse edges read about 55 ns.
  • Level: about −52 dBm at the SM200B with the horn 7 m from the racon (chain gain −27.8 dB, so about −24 dBm at the horn port). The horn gain is not known yet, so no racon EIRP is given.

Each element's frequency is the phase slope over its middle 80 %; the Furuno pulse's frequency is measured the same way in the same snippet, so the offset does not depend on the SM200B's tuning. Peak = mode of a 0.1 MHz histogram smoothed over 0.5 MHz. Table: radar_test/racon/data/racon_freq_offset.csv.

Interactive raw I/Q viewer: the whole 250 MS/s horn recording (every sample of all 2671 snippets; zoom on a selection, pan, step reply by reply, jump to the Furuno pulse).

In the Furuno-referenced row the I/Q rotation rate is the racon-minus-Furuno offset: the long R dash makes about 25 turns in 25.7 us (+0.95 MHz). Script radar_test/racon/racon_iq.py; plotted samples in radar_test/racon/data/racon_iq_examples.csv.

Timing: Morse element lengths, gaps and delay
Short R: 0.75x timing, sent as one 18-reply block per Furuno beam pass
  • The gap that cuts into the dash in the stacked plots is the short R. It is the same Morse R played 0.75 times as long, so it is over by 45 us while the long R is still in its dash.
  • It is not random. It comes as one solid block of about 18 replies in a row (about 28 ms) once per burst, at a different place in each burst, and then a few stray short replies 5 to 15 replies later. Every block is in radar_test/racon/data/racon_short_blocks.csv.
  • 28 ms is about 3.9 degrees of the radar's 2.59 s turn, roughly the width of the radar's main beam. Inside the block the racon answers sooner (1.34 us, very steady, against 1.72 us with a wide spread) and the radar reads about 7 dB stronger at the SM200B. Both point the same way: the short R is the answer to the radar's main beam, and the long R is the answer to its sidelobes. The racon is only 15 m from the radar, so the sidelobes are strong enough to trigger it all round the turn.
  • Not proven: the radar level is measured at the SM200B, not at the racon, and the radar's beamwidth has not been measured. The stray short replies after the block may be a near sidelobe. The SeaBeacon manual may say whether it shortens its code on strong interrogations.
Edges: 10-90 % rise and fall times

Single replies are too noisy at 250 MS/s to time an edge, so every reply is lined up on its own half-power crossing and averaged. The short spike right at each racon edge in the average may be a real turn-on/turn-off transient or a side effect of lining up on a noisy crossing; not yet decided.

Furuno pulses in these recordings
Sweeps 0.1-20 GHz; Furuno 2nd harmonic
  • Horn at the radar, both on: strongest line 9403.7 MHz, −38.6 dBm at the SM200B (swept, so it reads lower than the I/Q peak).
  • 2nd harmonic seen: 18806.8 MHz, −63.0 dBm at the SM200B with the horn on the radar, exactly twice the radar frequency. Not seen (below −87 dBm) with the horn on the racon. The chain's loss at 18.8 GHz is not known (LNA, limiter, horn), so this is not yet a level at the antenna.
  • 0.1-20 GHz: besides the radar only 1855 MHz and 2.4-2.56 GHz lines (phones, Wi-Fi). The wide sweep is slow and misses most short pulses, which is why the harmonic is not in it.
  • The 3rd harmonic (28.2 GHz) is above the SM200B's 20 GHz.

Racon 9 Nov: every analysis plot (per capture, per segment, the sweeps and the summary figures)

All plots made from the 9 Nov racon session that were not yet on this tab: per-capture chain, loudness, replies, stats and timeline; the stacked statistics; the band sweeps (9–10 GHz, second harmonic, wide); the summary figures (frequency offset, durations, edges, levels, short block, I/Q against time); and the synthetic-data checks. The raw recordings (.npz, several GB) stay on the clinic computer; the interactive I/Q viewer is at racon_iq/.

Script radar_test/racon/racon_capture.py says:

Record the Furuno and the racon with the SM200B (Python API only; Spike must be closed). Run from anywhere.

    python racon_capture.py go              # everything below in order, then the plots. This is the normal call.
    python racon_capture.py check           # 3 s at 9.4026 GHz, max attenuation: peak level, headroom to +20 dBm, noise
    python racon_capture.py survey [-s 10]  # 9.0-10.0 GHz sweeps, max hold and a waterfall: where is the racon replying?
    python racon_capture.py seg [-n 8]      # segmented I/Q, 160 MHz wide, video trigger, 250 snippets per capture
    python racon_capture.py stream [-s 30]  # continuous 50 MS/s I/Q, every event's time and level, snippets of the first 4000
    add --tag load to any of them for the 50 ohm load test (antenna replaced by a load: shows what leaks straight into the SM200B)
    add --center 9.45e9 if the survey shows the racon somewhere else

Every capture is saved in data/<mode>_<tag>_<time>/ as it comes in, so a USB drop loses at most one capture.
Safety: check refuses to go on if anything is within 10 dB of the SM200B's +20 dBm limit.

Script radar_test/racon/racon_figs.py says:

One figure per idea, every recording with racon replies pooled (run after racon_stats.py; reads its CSVs).

    python racon_figs.py           # all figures (re-reads the 250 MS/s captures for the edge figure, about a minute)
    python racon_figs.py --no-edges

Writes plots/racon_fig1_durations.png, _fig2_edges, _fig3_frequency, _fig4_levels, _fig5_short_block, and
data/racon_short_blocks.csv (one row per block of short R replies).

I and Q of single racon replies against time, from the 250 MS/s horn recording (seg_horn_racon_250M).

Writes plots/racon_fig6_iq_time.png and data/racon_iq_examples.csv (the plotted samples).

VNA readings

Every network analyzer (HP 8720ES) measurement, with the setup photos, gathered from the part tabs. The same plots and tables also stay on each part’s own tab.

Power limiter HLM-20PSM (EVAL-HLM-20P board), 31 Oct; also on the Limiter tab

VNA small-signal sweep (8720ES, 31 Oct): EVAL-HLM-20P board, use these

Delta markers off, cal not interpolated (C2 on screen). Includes the evaluation board’s connectors and traces.

MarkerFrequencyS21 (loss)S12S11 (in match)S22 (out match)
150 MHz−0.099 dB−0.067 dB−36.16 dB−39.13 dB
48.008 GHz−1.617 dB−1.166 dB−12.29 dB−15.04 dB
29.400 GHz (radar band)−1.759 dB−1.670 dB−14.40 dB−13.14 dB
310.000 GHz−1.697 dB−1.943 dB−13.40 dB−11.36 dB
520.046 GHz−2.237 dB−2.216 dB−18.05 dB−23.64 dB
  • Loss at 9.4 GHz is about 1.7 dB, against the datasheet’s 0.5 dB typical, 0.7 dB at 10 GHz and 1.5 dB max. The datasheet figures are for the limiter; how much of the extra is the evaluation board was not measured. This replaces the over-the-air 0.8 dB, which was already marked untrustworthy.
  • Match at 9.4 GHz is 13–14 dB return loss (datasheet 15 dB typical).
  • S21 and S12 agree within 0.09 dB at 9.4 GHz, but differ by up to 0.45 dB at 8 GHz. The S11 trace is noticeably noisier than S22, so the port 1 connection is worth checking.
  • This is a low-level measurement. It says nothing about clamping.

Earlier VNA sweep: relative readings, superseded

Screens were in delta-marker mode with an interpolated cal (C2Δ, 1601 points), so these are dB relative to a fixed marker whose value is not on screen. Do not read them as loss. Differences within a column are valid: S21 falls 1.7 dB from 50 MHz to 9.4 GHz. S21 and S12 differ by 0.6–1.1 dB at every marker, more than a reciprocal part should; the 10 dB pad, taken on the same setup, shows the same offset, so suspect the setup. This low-level sweep says nothing about clamping.

Attenuator pads 3, 6 and 10 dB; also on the Radar tab

Agilent 8720ES, 85052D kit (3.5 mm), full 2-port cal: 50 MHz–20.05 GHz, 801 points, IF BW 1 kHz, −10 dBm. Cal REG26 was made with the first cable; recalibrated with the better cable for the sweeps below. All values in dB. Copy-paste version: radar_test/vna/pad_measurements.csv. 3 dB pad, sweep 3 (marker readings, better cable, recalibrated; use these):

FrequencyS21 (loss)S12S11 (in match)S22 (out match)
50 MHz−2.943 dB−2.932 dB−49.61 dB−48.01 dB
8.008 GHz−3.505 dB−3.707 dB−20.20 dB−23.12 dB
9.400 GHz (radar band)−3.608 dB−3.939 dB−19.88 dB−15.20 dB
10.000 GHz−3.564 dB−3.749 dB−16.46 dB−16.68 dB
20.048 GHz−5.369 dB−5.085 dB−6.86 dB−8.84 dB
  • At 9.4 GHz the “3 dB” pad loses 3.6–3.9 dB, about 0.6–0.9 dB more than its label. It is rated only to 8 GHz.
  • S21 and S12 differ by 0.33 dB at 9.4 GHz. A passive pad is reciprocal, so that difference is measurement error, and it sets the uncertainty of these numbers.
  • The cable mattered: the same pad read 4.18 dB at 9.5 GHz on the first cable (sweep 2) and 3.6 dB at 9.4 GHz on this one.
  • Sweep 1 showed an S21 notch to −10 dB and an S22 spike to ~0 dB near 5.7 GHz. That is more power out than in (|S21|² + |S22|² > 1), so it was not the pad; it is gone in sweeps 2 and 3. Sweep 1 readings were by eye and are superseded.

10 dB pad: relative readings only, to be retaken

These screens were in delta-marker mode (ΔREF=Δ), so the numbers below are relative to a fixed reference marker, not absolute dB. Differences within one column are valid. The reference value is not on the screens. Fitting the photos suggests about −14.6 dB (the last 6 dB pad S22 reading), which would put S21 near −10.7 and S12 near −11.3 dB at 9.4 GHz, but that is an estimate. S21 and S12 then differ by a nearly constant 0.5–0.8 dB, including at 50 MHz, so do not use these as loss values.

Vivaldi antenna S11; also on the Radar tab

Vivaldi on port 1 of the 8720ES, nothing on port 2. Delta markers off, cal not interpolated (C2 on screen). Turning the antenna around changed the earlier trace only slightly. Use these numbers:

Test gear

Syscomp CGR-201
QuantityValue

Offset step1.875 mV per code
Amplitude step1.33 to 1.40 mV pk-pk per code

ConnectionUSB serial, COM12, 115200 baud
  • With a waveform selected and amplitude 0 it still outputs about 100 mV pk-pk of that waveform. For DC the waveform must be switched off.
  • It returns to default settings when its USB is unplugged.

Scope

QuantityValue

Input1 MΩ ∥ 20 pF; 50 V peak max (label)

Accuracy check, 26 Octread 1.1429 V where the meter read 1.139 V (4 mV)
Accuracy check, 1 Novinput A 4–8 mV above the meter. Input B 1.4–1.7 % low, offset drifting −7.5 → −2.5 mV over 75 min; follows input B when leads are swapped (calibration). Use rises, not absolute values
  • Protocol from Syscomp’s command list and the Yelloscope source (github.com/johnpeck/yelloscope). Its calibration is read from its EEPROM with e commands; never send E (write).

ADALM-Pluto SDR
  • Used as a 1.0–1.2 GHz source in September.
  • Maximum output +11 dBm = 12.6 mW (team notes).
  • Measured 12 Oct: about 0 dBm at attenuation 0 dB and tone scale 0.5. See the Pluto tab.
  • Soapy sink (Homebrew GNU Radio): gain 0–89 dB. Gain g sets the AD9364 TX attenuation to 89 − g dB exactly (register read back 26 Oct).
  • 26 Oct, through the envelope detector: 0.0 dBm at 0 dB, tone scale 0.7, 1100 MHz, Soapy sink. 2.6 dB under what the Pluto tab predicts; see the Envelope detector tab.
  • It dropped off USB twice on 26 Oct while sharing an unpowered hub with the CGR-201 (500 mA for both). Plug it straight into the computer.
  • There are at least two Pluto units (serials …f3647c41f6 and …dd1f84bfdb). On 1 Nov the second read 0.4 dB lower at 1.1 GHz than the first. Calibrate per unit and note the serial (system_profiler SPUSBDataType).
  • At full output (0 dB, tone scale 0.7) a Pluto TX spur at −3 × the tone offset, about −25 dBc, beats with the tone (400 kHz ripple through the envelope detector, 1 Nov).
  • GNU Radio flowgraphs: pluto_simple_tx.grc, soapy_simple_tx.grc.

Mixer on its own: voltage against frequency, wide and 900 to 1200 MHz
  • This joins two different measurements, the VCO sweep of 10 Oct and the Pluto sweeps of 16 Sep. Sources, powers and meters differ, so they are not one curve.
  • No data from 920 to 1000 MHz. A single sweep from 700 to 1600 MHz with the amps out has not been taken.
  • Voltage depends strongly on power: at 1080 MHz it changes from 45.7 to 8.3 mV over 10 dB of Pluto setting. So no single table works without a fixed power.
  • Data: phase_detector_calibration/lut_mixer_alone.csv. The table for the 744 to 788 MHz part is in the next section.
4 x ZX60-P162LN+ then the mixer: voltage against frequency, wide and 900 to 1200 MHz
  • Power from -40 dBm up to -33 dBm, the highest measured from 880 to 1200 MHz (-30 dBm needed less than the Pluto's 31 dB attenuation floor there, so it has no points).
  • Worst case, 950 to 1010 MHz: 17.8 mV of voltage band (at 996 MHz), which is a 5 MHz span of possible frequencies. Typical span 2 MHz.
  • Of that, power alone within one run gives 12.3 to 13.5 mV and 4 MHz; the same level measured twice, 3 hours apart, differs by up to 6.7 mV and 3 MHz.
  • Below about 950 MHz the curve is flat (about 0.9 mV/MHz), so the same band means up to 25 MHz near 900 MHz. Above about 1015 MHz the curve is flat and then turns over, so a reading there does not give one frequency.
  • Steady tone from the Pluto only; radar pulses not yet measured on this chain.
  • Steady tone from the Pluto. Not yet measured with the radar's pulses.
  • The straight part is about 960 to 1010 MHz: 2.57 mV/MHz, within 2.2 mV rms of a line. 900 to 950 MHz is also close to straight at 0.87 mV/MHz. 900 to 1200 MHz as a whole is not linear (40 mV rms off a line).
  • The curve first stops rising at about 1065 MHz, so one voltage gives one frequency only below that, and only 900 to about 1020 MHz has a useful slope.
  • Power alone, 1 MHz sweeps at -65 to -36 dBm: from 960 to 1010 MHz the levels differ by 10.8 mV on average and 16.7 mV at most, which is about 4 and 6.5 MHz of frequency error at 2.57 mV/MHz. From 900 to 950 MHz they differ by 9.4 mV on average, about 11 MHz at 0.87 mV/MHz.
  • Below -65 dBm the curves leave the rail.

How to use it

  1. Read the mixer output voltage V in mV.
  2. Find the two rows on either side of it (the table is sorted by mixer voltage).
  3. Draw a straight line between them and read the VCO frequency f in MHz. The slope column is the MHz per mV between neighbouring rows.
\[ f(V) = f_i + (V - V_i)\,\frac{f_{i+1} - f_i}{V_{i+1} - V_i} \]
Code
use = cal[cal["vt_meas_v"] <= 1.2]             # the part where voltage only rises with frequency
mhz, mv = use["vco_freq_hz"] / 1e6, use["mixer_out_v"] * 1e3
order = np.argsort(mv)

def mv_to_mhz(x):
    return np.interp(x, mv[order], mhz[order])

How it was made: see Mixer, Mixer look up table.

Tests to run

Rules before any test
  • Read the maximum input power on the Signal Hound SM200B label. Do not exceed it.
  • Put a fixed attenuator before the SM200B whenever an amplifier is in the path.
  • Use a DC block if the part under test can put DC on its output.
  • Do not connect the Furuno radar to anything by cable. It is 2.2 kW peak. Radar tests are over the air only.
What the computer can control

Siglent SSA3021XUSBsweep to 2.1 GHz, read peak frequency and powerworking
Siglent SDS1104X-EUSBread DC levels and waveforms to 100 MHzworking
Syscomp CGR-201USBDC to 3.52 V, square waves; two-channel scope capturesworking
ADALM-PlutoUSBtone at 325 MHz–3.8 GHzworking; see the Pluto tab

Not decided: the source for 9.3–9.5 GHz test signals. Options: (1) a second ADF5355 at 9.4 GHz, (2) Pluto at 1.0–1.2 GHz into the TX mixer with the 8.3 GHz LO, (3) the radar over the air. Option 2 can be swept by the computer.

Syscomp output not steady at amplitude 0
Syscomp settingVt rippleAnalyzer shows
Square selected, amplitude 048 mV rms, 116 mV pk-pktwo peaks, 769.7 and 773.1 MHz
Waveform off2 mV rms (scope noise)one peak, 771.4 MHz
  • Affected: calibration runs 1 and 2, the first noise test, the partial sweep with the open tee, and the static curve of 10 Oct morning.
  • Their frequencies are wrong by −1.75 to +0.40 MHz.
  • Fixed by switching the waveform off. Run 3 and everything after it is correct.

Analyzer marker read before the sweep finished
  • Power readings jumped by 15 dB between neighbouring points.
  • Fixed by doing one complete sweep before each reading.
  • After the fix, six readings in a row agreed within 0.1 dB and 0.03 MHz.
  • The open tee port was wrongly blamed for this at first.
Open tee port
  • The first wiring had a second tee with one port left open. It was replaced with a male-male adaptor.
  • 15 points were recorded with the open port before the change.
  • With the port closed the VCO ran 1.5 to 3.2 MHz lower at the same voltage.
  • Both plots were taken before the Syscomp fix. Frequencies are wrong by up to 1.7 MHz. The power panel in the second plot is the early-reading error and is not valid.

                                phase_detector_calibration/plot_pd_design_limits.py — What limits the phase detector, and what to change to read frequency to +/-2 MHz over 200 MHz (19 Nov). Four questions: 1. How weak may the weakest pulse be? Lo (100 lines)

                                What limits the phase detector, and what to change to read frequency to +/-2 MHz over 200 MHz (19 Nov). Four questions: 1. How weak may the weakest pulse be? Longest stretch with total width <= 4 MHz (Sorin's method, plot_pd_x_uncertainty.measure) against the threshold level, every run with two or more levels. 2. What does the power dependence look like? pad10hf: each level's reading minus the railed median curve M, every frequency. 3. Is it power or drift? Every pass of every padded run fitted against M over the whole band: d = a (M - mean M) - s M' + c, a = gain change (%), s = shift of the curve along frequency (MHz), c = DC offset (mV). Vectorised least squares, all passes at once. Passes at the same level that agree mean a systematic power effect, not drift. 4. What would another cable do? Gain, shift and offset errors all become frequency errors divided by the slope, which scales with tau, while the monotonic half-cycle shrinks as 1/tau. With r = tau_new / tau_now: width_new(phase) = width_now(phase) / r and span(r) = longest(width_now <= 4 r) / r, read off pad10hf's measured width (the only run with a clean half-cycle); plotted against the arm difference r x 24.7 cm, with every padded run's measured span as a dot. Assumes the level dependence stays the same in phase (set by the amplifiers and mixer, not the cable) and the pads keep reflections down. Saves pd_design_limits_19nov.png.

                                phase_detector_calibration/plot_pd_theory.py — Theory against measurement for every phase detector arrangement (Sorin, 19 Nov). An ideal delay-line phase detector gives V(f) = A cos(2 pi f tau) + C with tau (81 lines)

                                Theory against measurement for every phase detector arrangement (Sorin, 19 Nov). An ideal delay-line phase detector gives V(f) = A cos(2 pi f tau) + C with tau = (RF arm - LO arm) / (VF c). Constants ignored (Sorin): each panel shows only the cosine, -1 to +1, against frequency. theory: cos(2 pi f tau), tau from the measured cable lengths at an assumed VF 0.70 (typical PTFE coax), phase 0; measured: the run's strongest level, scaled so its own min..max spans -1..+1 (removes A and C; exaggerates a run that swings less than a full cycle); fit (less important): best single cosine, tau scanned 0.02-2.5 ns (pdlib.delay), scaled the same way as the measured data. Last panel: every theory cosine together. Saves pd_theory_vs_measured.png and prints the table.

                                phase_detector_calibration/plot_pd_x_uncertainty.py — Frequency uncertainty when the input power is unknown, Sorin's method (19 Nov), for every phase detector run. Level set = the Pluto levels from the highest down (151 lines)

                                Frequency uncertainty when the input power is unknown, Sorin's method (19 Nov), for every phase detector run. Level set = the Pluto levels from the highest down to a lower threshold. Lookup = the median curve of the set: at each frequency, the median of every reading of every level in the set. At each true frequency f, take the reading at the highest level and the reading at the threshold level (each the median over that level's passes), read both back through the median curve, and plot each read frequency minus f. Total width = the distance between the two (Sorin: +/-2 MHz = 4 MHz total). The lookup must be single valued, so it is split wherever the median curve turns; a reading past a turn has no unique frequency (marked x). Thresholds: every level, -60 dBm, the lowest railed level, -50 dBm. Two plots per run: voltage read against frequency (one line per Pluto level, every pass, every reading) with the median curves; then the frequency offsets. Usage: python plot_pd_x_uncertainty.py [tag ...]. Saves pd_x_uncertainty_<tag>.png per run, pd_x_uncertainty_all_runs.png and pd_x_uncertainty_table.json (the site's table).

                                • grid(rows, levels) rows (MHz, dBm, pass key, mV) -> f, level of each pass, array passes x f (NaN where a pass has no point). Only frequencies that every level in the set has.
                                • stretches(med) Index ranges [i, j] where the median curve keeps one direction.
                                • offsets(f, med, *V) Each reading curve in V read back through the median curve, minus the true frequency (MHz). The lookup is the monotonic stretch of the median curve that holds f; a reading outside that stretch's range has no unique frequency (NaN).
                                • measure(rows, L) Level set L -> f, median curve, offsets (top level, threshold level; MHz), total width, passes, longest stretch (n, a, b) with width <= 4 MHz.

                                                  Two-round DC reading on the SDS1104X-E with the finest V/div that holds the signal, so the 8-bit ADC adds no quantization (Sorin, 18 Nov: always the highest resolution; measure, then zoom in on that voltage and measure precisely). Round 1: coarse V/div gives the level and its noise. Round 2: centre the screen on that level (offset = -level) at the finest V/div whose +-4 div holds the noise; if any sample clips, step up one range and read again.

                                                  • class Tracker Zoomed readings along a sweep: per key (Pluto level) keep the last fine V/div and level, and read next time with the screen centred on the last level, so only the offset moves (no V/div switch, no coarse round). A clipped record, or no history, falls back to zoom_read. The V/div for the next point holds span_sd x the noise plus the last step in level.

                                                                          vco_rise_time/analysis.py — Signal processing for the VCO step-response test. (240 lines)

                                                                          Signal processing for the VCO step-response test.

                                                                          • expected_freq_hz(vt) Expected VCO frequency from the earlier spectrum-analyzer measurements.
                                                                          • datasheet_freq_hz(vt) Straight-line prediction used in the spreadsheet (0.8 GHz + 60 MHz/V).
                                                                          • edge_time(t, v, lo, hi, frac) First time v crosses lo + frac*(hi-lo) going up (linear interpolation).
                                                                          • levels(v) Low/high plateau levels of a two-level waveform.
                                                                          • rise_10_90(t, y, y0, y1) 10-90 % transition time of y going from y0 to y1 (either direction).
                                                                          • settle_time(t, y, y0, y1, tol) Last time y is outside +/- tol*(step) of its final value.
                                                                          • remove_periodic(t, v, edges, period) Subtract everything locked to the square wave (drive feedthrough) from v.
                                                                          • choose_band(fa_lo, fa_hi, fs, margin, max_lag) Pick (start, stop, taper_lo, taper_hi) and the lag for a step between two alias plateaus.
                                                                          • plateau_noise_psd(t, v, edges, fs, m) Noise density (variance per sample, vs frequency) from the settled stretches only.
                                                                          • lag_product(v, fs, band, lag, noise, avoid) z[n+lag] * conj(z[n]) for the analytic signal restricted to band = (start, stop).
                                                                          • lag_to_alias(p, fs, band_start, lag) Alias frequency from an (averaged) lag product, resolved inside the band.
                                                                          • stack_edges(tp, p, edges, grid) Sum p(t - edge) over all edges, interpolated onto the common grid.
                                                                          • rising_edges(t, v, lo, hi) Times of all low->high crossings of the 50 % level (with hysteresis).
                                                                          • smooth(x, n)
                                                                          • unfold(f_alias, fs, f_expected) Map alias frequency to the true frequency in the zone containing f_expected.
                                                                          • fold(f_true, fs) Alias frequency of f_true when sampled at fs.
                                                                          • class LevelStack Accumulates all rising edges of one voltage level into a frequency-vs-time trace.

                                                                          File locations

                                                                          Every Panthalassa data set: where it is on the clinic computer, where its copy is on the USB backup drive, how big it is, and the bench setup and instrument settings it was taken with. Sizes and dates are read from the disk at each build of this site. Everything is inside the Dropbox clinic folder C:\ThatFamily Dropbox\Sorin Jayaweera\allSaves\mudd\senior\clinic except the raw racon recordings in C:\racon_raw.

                                                                          • USB backup: E:\Panthalassa_backup, made by clinic\claude\backup_to_usb.ps1 (re-run any time; it adds and updates, never deletes). It holds the whole clinic folder except the 276 GB raw racon recordings, which need a drive of 512 GB or more.
                                                                          • This list is also saved as clinic\claude\FILE_LOCATIONS.html (one file, opens in any browser) and copied to the USB drive.
                                                                          • Power columns in the CSVs say whether they are measured at the instrument or measured plus the pads (for example measured + 29 dB).
                                                                          Phase detector: Delay-line phase detector sweeps 13–18 Nov (all bench configurations)

                                                                          Setup: Pluto TX → 7 cm → 4 × ZX60-P162LN+ (7 cm between, Agilent E3630A about 4.03 V, 0.23 A) → 7 cm → ZFRSC-42-S+ splitter → right arm (LO) cable D 16.6 cm, left arm (RF) cable B 15.2 cm + C (about 12 cm) or E with adapter (about 9 cm) → ZX05-30W-S+ mixer → IF to SDS1104X-E CH1 (1 MΩ, DC) and, through 20 dB of pads, the SM200B. Each configuration (cables, pads, IF cable, IF load) is one row of pd_runs.py, listed below.

                                                                          Instrument settings: Pluto CW 600–1600 MHz (wide runs 300–4000 MHz) at −36 to −71 dBm, attenuation never under the 31 dB floor; scope CH1 mean of the IF in mV; tone-off readings as stage off.

                                                                          Review notes

                                                                          Marks and comments made by people on the GitHub copy of this page. Each one is a GitHub issue in Sorin-Jayaweera/Panthalassa-Clinic-Team, written with that person's own GitHub account.

                                                                          How to add one

                                                                          1. Open the GitHub copy of this page and press Edit in the bar at the top.
                                                                          2. Select some text. A small bar appears: Validated, Under question, Comment, Suggest a change.
                                                                          3. Press one. GitHub opens with the quote filled in. Add a note if you want and press Submit new issue.
                                                                          4. Reload this page. The text is highlighted and the note is listed below. The folder review/ in the repository is updated about a minute later.

                                                                          To withdraw a mark, or when a question has been answered, close the issue on GitHub.

                                                                          Loading.

                                                                          Hand-written notes (gold)

                                                                          Text highlighted like this was written by a person, not generated. All of it lives in one file, docs/human_notes.html in the repository (edit it on GitHub). Each <section data-for="ID">...</section> in it shows up at the top of the tab or section with that id (data-pos="bottom" for the end). Any HTML works inside. Rebuilding the site never changes that file; a note stays until someone edits or deletes it.

                                                                            • pd-day-18nov 18 Nov, every arrangement and what it showed: the ~360 MHz pattern is the mixer ports' reflections coming back through the resistive splitter
                                                                            • pd-amp-chain Amplifier chain alone into the SM200B: is the ~360 MHz pattern already in the amplifiers? (18 Nov from 13:06): its amplitude ripple does not match, but that does not rule the amplifiers out (Sorin)
                                                                            • pd-short-cables Very short cables at every mixer connection, 50 ohm load on the IF (18 Nov 10:39-12:40): pattern unchanged
                                                                            • pd-delay The ‘ripple’ is the interferometer itself: the arms differ by about 2.75 ns, not 0.55 ns (16 Nov)
                                                                            • pd-vs-pluto Is the ~360 MHz pattern the Pluto’s own level ripple? No (16 Nov)
                                                                            • pd-ifs Short IF cable (15 Nov night): the ~360 MHz ripple is NOT caused by the long IF cable; densest data so far
                                                                            • pd-hd-night Pads removed, long IF cable: 600–1600 MHz at three levels (15 Nov, 20:03–20:31)
                                                                            • pd-no-pads Pads removed (15 Nov evening): twice the swing, and the curve moves about 110 MHz
                                                                            • pd-five-levels Five Pluto levels across 1150–1550 MHz, coarse to fine (14 Nov evening): the rise runs 1215–1445 MHz with no flat sides; −36 to −57 dBm agree within ±2 MHz on 90% of it
